dec:001.title: Decision 001: The 2018 text is Creative Commons BY
dec:001.said: "The license of this is going to be this as before, CC by, Creative Commons by."

dec:002.title: Decision 002: Leanpub gets our own PDF, built here and matched to the 2018 one
dec:002.said: "I want to try to upload LeanPub, the print PDF. I want to see if that can work. So we can do everything here." And: "compare with the print PDF created by LeanPub, and we should be able to match it here."

dec:003.title: Decision 003: Every format from one source
dec:003.said: "I would like to create them all here from the same source."

dec:004.title: Decision 004: The cover waits
dec:004.said: "We'll make a decision on the cover a bit later on."

dec:005.title: Decision 005: Text issues live in the vault
dec:005.said: "For now, all the text issues we'll leave in our vault. So we're going to move into the vault, and we can start with that V2.0, because it's just been released."

dec:006.title: Decision 006: Every change is minor, unless Dinis says it is major
dec:006.said: "Every change should be minor, unless I say it's a major one."

dec:007.title: Decision 007: Two kinds of article
dec:007.said: "We need to have an article, which is article where I write or we co-write together, like where it's speaking in my voice. And I think you should have another article, which is where you write it with updates, and actually every agent writes with the updates."

dec:008.title: Decision 008: The book is made in release mode, through a review board
dec:008.said: "Let's do the book in release mode, right? So can we have a first release candidate of the book?" And: "let's create a sort of adversarial sort of review board where once we got that first release candidate, then every word, every change, every idea that we're going to add to the book needs to go through that sort of process."

dec:009.title: Decision 009: A release candidate is read on the site from a frozen snapshot, marked, and is not a version
dec:009.said: "Let's do a release of it and see what it looks like. [...] Our first release candidate for the book, which should be an end-to-end book, fully built, with introduction. [...] Let's basically put that there, and then see where we are, and then I can read it, and then I'll print it out, and then I'll start providing feedback on those materials."

dec:010.title: Decision 010: The title is Gen Z Developers (GenAI Edition)
dec:010.said: "The name of the book is 'Gen Z Developers (GenAI Edition)'."

dec:011.title: Decision 011: Precedents go on a list Dinis can overturn, and Dinis reads the diffs
dec:011.said: "Yes, the list can overturn. And basically, you have to remember that I would also be reading the diffs, right, of the book, which is a very important concept here. So I can keep an eye on it."

dec:012.title: Decision 012: The book is 200 pages or more
dec:012.said: "The book actually should be, you know, much bigger. I think, in a way, that book was quite thin. We need to easily, you know, we should be hitting the 200 plus pages."

dec:013.title: Decision 013: The hands-on part is in the release candidate
dec:013.said: "The hands-on, we'll start adding that. Actually, we need to start putting in the release candidate of what we want in there."

dec:014.title: Decision 014: The title is Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition)
dec:014.said: "Ok agreed, let's go with "Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition)"."

dec:015.title: Decision 015: The Gen ZX proposal is the frame of release candidate 2
dec:015.said: "I think we're already ready for RC2, because if you pull from the repo, you'll find the new positioning, which I think is very exciting [...] can you basically recreate the book taking that into account, and the new title and the new positioning and the content that we want to add? [...] now we have two generations and we really focus now on that whole idea of creating a company, right? The whole idea of creating a Gen AI company, a startup, and that's my target audience."

topic:everyone-is-a-developer.title: Everyone who can brief an agent is a developer now
topic:everyone-is-a-developer.why: The opening frame of the edition: the reader is already a developer if they can describe what they want to an agent; Gen Z in 2026, the citizen developer, your own language as a programming language, and optimism against the burnout mood.

topic:explorers-villagers-town-planners.title: Explorers, villagers and town planners (Wardley's frame)
topic:explorers-villagers-town-planners.why: The structure of the whole book: where the reader sits, what explorer coding is good for, and the handover to people who maintain and answer for software; the 2018 pioneers/settlers/town planners outline grown up.

topic:getting-the-job.title: Getting the job: hired for the workflow, act as the job you want
topic:getting-the-job.why: The practical promise of the book: why October 2026 is a moment of opportunity, what employers want (AI operators), how to stand out when candidates look equal, and how to work in public so others can help you.

topic:publish-in-public.title: Publish, publish, publish: your own newsroom
topic:publish-in-public.why: Linkable work is the CV now: a site published by an agent from voice memos, an article behind every answer, small finished pieces over big batches.

topic:working-with-agents.title: How to work with agents: briefs, voice, one shared state
topic:working-with-agents.why: The day-to-day craft: brief by voice, review on the phone, focused sessions with roles, lessons and debriefs as memory, a daily brief, and reading sources in full.

topic:facts-and-the-record.title: Facts, evidence and the record
topic:facts-and-the-record.why: Make fact-based decisions (on the 2018 cover) in the agent era: think out loud and let the record check you, count rather than remember, review as a record, and distrust self-reports.

topic:human-in-the-loop.title: Where a person belongs: one-way doors, two-way doors and blast radius
topic:human-in-the-loop.why: The judgement a newcomer needs before letting an agent act: how cheap is it to undo, how large is the blast radius, and how the record moves the line over time.

topic:controlling-your-agent.title: Controlling your agent: mandate, reach and hope versus enforcement
topic:controlling-your-agent.why: Before you give an agent access, write down what it is for and what it can reach; rules in a prompt are hope, rules in a hook or platform are enforcement; behaviour, decision and workflow are different questions.

topic:security-agent-era.title: Security for the agent era: least code, supply chain, secrets, learning to hack
topic:security-agent-era.why: Code is a liability; the next maintainer is an agent; check skills and dependencies before installing; keep secrets out of the chat; learning to hack is still how you learn how things work.

topic:open-source.title: Open source: contribute, fork, and why it protects everyone
topic:open-source.why: Open source remains the newcomer's best door (first PR, public work) and is becoming the most secure software; the fork protects founders, customers and investors; constraints make better products.

topic:building-blocks.title: Building blocks: cloud, serverless, free models, git and CI
topic:building-blocks.why: What a non-specialist can assemble today, mostly free, with an agent doing the one-time setup; git as a standard; CI; knowing what tokens cost.

topic:graphs-memory.title: Graphs, memory and your future self
topic:graphs-memory.why: Graphs as the way of thinking (not just Dot): brief from a graph, maintain it rather than perfect it, search as navigation; and keep your work linkable and backed up so your future self can find it.

topic:be-a-founder.title: Be a founder (or a one-person service)
topic:be-a-founder.why: Agents make execution cheap, so the expert can build first; what investors select for; technology that works before the use case; small agent-run services and pay-after-value models.

topic:civic-and-history.title: Civic responsibility: hacking a country, sovereignty, your language
topic:civic-and-history.why: Dinis's Portugal talks as the then-now of civic responsibility: to hack means to solve problems; what regulation delivered; small countries can lead in code now that everyone can build.

topic:making-of.title: How this book was made (the last part)
topic:making-of.why: The edition's own workflow as the final worked example: repository and vault, agents in roles, voice memos, the record, review on the record, three voices, co-written with Claude and the memo-to-word ratio.

topic:direction-is-the-scarce-skill.title: Direction is the scarce skill: the place of highest leverage, knowing when to stop, starting without knowing the end
topic:direction-is-the-scarce-skill.why: When anyone can brief an agent, building stops being the bottleneck and choosing what to build, and when to stop, becomes the skill employers and users pay for. This is the junior's version of seniority, and it answers the 2018 life-patterns outlines (habits, the zone, start with why) that had no article.

topic:your-first-workspace.title: Your first workspace: from one Claude Project to a team of agents, safely
topic:your-first-workspace.why: The first pass flagged this as gap 1, with no how-to in scope. Four imported articles together make a step-by-step path: a folder per person in Drive with a Claude Project, then habits, then the agent's own mailbox and seat, with agents kept off your laptop. It could also sit as the opening chapter of working-with-agents.

topic:shipped-means-the-user-has-it.title: Shipped means the user has it: tests, CI and going slow to go fast
topic:shipped-means-the-user-has-it.why: Fills the testing/TDD gap with stories rather than theory. A green build is not a release, tests that never run are not tests, the handover from explorer to villager is a refactor you can prove, and synthetic users check what the user sees. Answers 2018 TDD, CI-Testing, SRE and devops.

concept:explorer-villager-town-planner.title: explorer / villager / town planner
concept:explorer-villager-town-planner.definition: Simon Wardley's three kinds of people and work: explorers build the new by trying, villagers harden and maintain what people start to depend on, town planners industrialise it and answer for it in production.

concept:explorer-coding.title: explorer coding
concept:explorer-coding.definition: The newsroom's name for vibe coding: anyone with a need explores it by building, with the fast feedback loop that made spreadsheets win; not ready to be 'in line' until villagers and town planners take it on.

concept:the-handover-deployment-gap.title: the handover (deployment gap)
concept:the-handover-deployment-gap.definition: The step from a prototype to a tool people rely on is not a place to stop but a handover from explorers to villagers and town planners, who add the non-functional requirements.

concept:citizen-developer.title: citizen developer
concept:citizen-developer.definition: The employee, owner or expert who now builds full applications: the spreadsheet grown up, good news rather than a risk.

concept:the-prototype-is-the-best-brief.title: the prototype is the best brief
concept:the-prototype-is-the-best-brief.definition: What someone builds for themselves says what they actually want, in a form that runs, better than any requirements document.

concept:ai-operator.title: AI operator
concept:ai-operator.definition: Dinis's term for the people companies need now: not model builders but people who use the tools and workflows to get things done.

concept:hired-for-the-workflow.title: hired for the workflow
concept:hired-for-the-workflow.definition: Being hired for the ability to run agentic workflows, as people were once hired for breaking apps or building websites, degree or no degree; the edge shows when candidates look equal, starting with the application.

concept:act-as-the-job-you-want.title: act as the job you want
concept:act-as-the-job-you-want.definition: If you are looking for a job you have time: do the job before you have it, in public, so it can be linked: reach does not matter, the link lets the people who want to help you forward it.

concept:your-own-newsroom.title: your own newsroom
concept:your-own-newsroom.definition: A personal publishing loop: voice memo in, an agent researches, checks and writes in your voice, a validated static site out, readers pay a little if it is useful.

concept:omnichannel-programming.title: omnichannel programming
concept:omnichannel-programming.definition: Programming across voice, chat, phone, IDE and pull requests where every channel reads and writes one shared state (git, vaults, briefs, graphs), as against multichannel, where each keeps its own copy.

concept:brief.title: brief
concept:brief.definition: A written request an agent session can start from: what is asked, what exists, what remains; the unit of work between a person and agents.

concept:one-way-door-two-way-door.title: one-way door / two-way door
concept:one-way-door-two-way-door.definition: Amazon's test, used here for agents: a two-way door can be undone cheaply (a page correction), a one-way door cannot (a sent email); the cost of undoing decides where a person belongs.

concept:blast-radius.title: blast radius
concept:blast-radius.definition: What an output or a row of an agent's reach would cost if it went wrong in full today; put the person where it is large and the output cannot be undone (defined fully in footprint-and-blast-radius, outside the surveyed set).

concept:agent-behaviour-policy-abp.title: Agent Behaviour Policy (ABP)
concept:agent-behaviour-policy-abp.definition: For one agent in one deployment: what it can reach, what it was authorised to do, the gap between the two, and what actually stands in the way of each capability.

concept:mandate-reach-and-the-gap.title: mandate, reach and the gap
concept:mandate-reach-and-the-gap.definition: Mandate is what the agent (or credential) is for; reach is everything it can touch; the gap between them is the risk, and every supply-chain attack used it.

concept:hope-based-security.title: hope-based security
concept:hope-based-security.definition: Rules written in a prompt and kept only if the model keeps them: better than nothing, not enough on its own.

concept:hooks.title: hooks
concept:hooks.definition: Small programs the agent's harness runs at fixed points (before and after a tool call, on prompt, on stop) that can see, block or rewrite actions; guardrails, not walls.

concept:behaviour-decision-and-workflow-.title: behaviour, decision and workflow policies
concept:behaviour-decision-and-workflow-.definition: Behaviour says what an agent may do, decision says who chooses at a branch point and on what evidence, workflow says in what order.

concept:allowed-is-not-right.title: allowed is not right
concept:allowed-is-not-right.definition: Every control can pass and the outcome still be wrong (a $150 refund where $120 was owed); proving the right outcome needs a written definition of right.

concept:lethal-trifecta.title: lethal trifecta
concept:lethal-trifecta.definition: Simon Willison's term the newsroom uses: private data, untrusted content and a way out in one agent or skill; any agent with all three needs a control even if honest.

concept:the-record.title: the record
concept:the-record.definition: What was actually done, kept outside anyone's memory (commits, briefs, transcripts, versions); 'the record catches up with the instinct', so thinking out loud becomes safe, and peer review moves to before publishing (confirmed, corrected or not found).

concept:review-on-the-record.title: review on the record
concept:review-on-the-record.definition: Every review is a file written once against published criteria, and every finding is answered: fixed in which version, declined and why, or open.

concept:self-report.title: self-report
concept:self-report.definition: An agent's own logs and account of itself; evidence written outside the agent is more honest and still needs reading.

concept:code-is-a-liability-minimal-viab.title: code is a liability / minimal viable code path
concept:code-is-a-liability-minimal-viab.definition: Every shipped line is a capability someone may misuse; the future is the smallest code that does exactly the job, made safe by model-built tests and maps.

concept:ephemeral-town-planner-services.title: ephemeral town planner services
concept:ephemeral-town-planner-services.definition: A better name for serverless: scales to zero, costs nothing idle, starts fast, a commodity exposed for others; test: if it bills you by the hour when idle, it is not serverless.

concept:fractal-semantic-graph.title: fractal semantic graph
concept:fractal-semantic-graph.definition: Knowledge held as a graph with an ontology and taxonomy per element, each part in its own vocabulary, every node openable as a graph of its own; briefs come from the slice you need.

concept:the-fork-next-door.title: the fork next door
concept:the-fork-next-door.definition: In open source anyone can fork, which protects founders, customers and investors from each other; forks take hold only when someone stops executing.

concept:every-part-buys-the-next.title: every part buys the next
concept:every-part-buys-the-next.definition: The subject buys the first line, the first line buys the paragraph, the paragraph buys the email: open with the short answer in plain text.

concept:three-voices.title: three voices
concept:three-voices.definition: Me alone, me through an agent, an agent in its own voice; every byline should say which.

concept:your-own-key.title: your own key
concept:your-own-key.definition: Using a model provider with your own API key called straight from the browser, so nobody else holds the key or pays for your questions.

concept:wardley-map.title: Wardley map
concept:wardley-map.definition: A graph with context in two directions: a value chain anchored on a user and a need, and an evolution axis (usually genesis, custom built, product, commodity, though the axis is a choice). Read out like a story, it says what to build, what to buy, and where a market exists. Every node is itself a map.

concept:place-of-highest-leverage.title: place of highest leverage
concept:place-of-highest-leverage.definition: Where the most value can be added now, nothing blocks you, and you can start without knowing how the whole problem ends. It is not where the biggest problem is. Each step is shipped and used before the next is chosen.

concept:direction-is-the-scarce-thing.title: direction is the scarce thing
concept:direction-is-the-scarce-thing.definition: Agents can build in any direction; what they cannot generate is the sense of what to build next and when to stop. People with a direction are the input to the loop, not displaced by it.

concept:knowing-when-to-stop.title: knowing when to stop
concept:knowing-when-to-stop.definition: The judgement that experience gives people (who the attackers are, the phase of the business, the bottleneck, what good enough looks like). Agents lack it by design, so it has to be supplied as constraints: a mandate, a stop named in advance, a narrow scope.

concept:footprint.title: footprint
concept:footprint.definition: What the agent actually did, read afterwards from the record and compared with its mandate. It is the partner of blast radius, which is what a reach would cost if used in full.

concept:green-does-not-mean-live.title: green does not mean live
concept:green-does-not-mean-live.definition: Shipped is a fact about the reader, not about your repository: a release has to check the boundary the user is on, not only the ones CI can see.

concept:an-agent-is-a-session-with-a-foc.title: an agent is a session with a focus
concept:an-agent-is-a-session-with-a-foc.definition: An agent is a named session (an @name) that reads a few documents about the project and a role.md saying what it does and does not do. One session per topic, never mixed threads.

concept:drafts-never-send.title: drafts, never send
concept:drafts-never-send.definition: The rule for an agentic inbox: agents read, label and draft, and a person reads, edits and presses send. The agent has its own mailbox and its own Claude seat, never yours.

concept:threat-ladder-draw-the-line-wher.title: threat ladder (draw the line where the attacker is)
concept:threat-ladder-draw-the-line-wher.definition: Security starts from who the threat agent is, the attack vector and how sophisticated it is. On a ladder from your own mistakes up to states, plan to the rung that matches what you protect, do the basics consistently, and write down what you accept above that rung.

concept:every-risk-is-already-accepted.title: every risk is already accepted
concept:every-risk-is-already-accepted.definition: Every risk an organisation has is already accepted by somebody, so the questions are who accepted it and until when.

concept:agents-decide-people-answer.title: agents decide, people answer
concept:agents-decide-people-answer.definition: Agents in loops make real decisions, but responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, because the grant is the moment of authorisation.

concept:agency-scale.title: agency scale
concept:agency-scale.definition: Seven levels from rubber stamp to the reviewer who fixes the source. A decision is capped by its weakest ingredient (options, context, time, incentives, escalation, authority). Below level 3 the person deciding carries liability without agency.

concept:every-mistake-added-a-rule.title: every mistake added a rule
concept:every-mistake-added-a-rule.definition: The complexity trap for agent operators: each mistake becomes a rule, the prompt grows, compaction comes sooner and new mistakes follow. The way out is small, tested, shipped components that move right on the map and no longer need the rule.

concept:re-anchoring.title: re-anchoring
concept:re-anchoring.definition: Keeping an agent's rules in a file that a hook prints back after every summary, so the rules are restored rather than remembered, with a canary that shows they are still being read.

concept:synthetic-users.title: synthetic users
concept:synthetic-users.definition: Invented people, each with a situation, a question, what they know and what makes them leave, played by a model that drives a real browser one screenshot at a time, so it can get lost as a person would.

concept:go-slow-to-go-fast.title: go slow to go fast
concept:go-slow-to-go-fast.definition: The explorer-to-villager move done as a pure refactor, proved by the live site serving the same bytes, before adding tests and hardening.

concept:no-server-by-design.title: no server by design
concept:no-server-by-design.definition: Retire the database (files), then the back end: encrypted vaults keep the server blind, the app runs in the browser, only commodity products are left on the server, and the gaps you accept are written down.

concept:do-they-miss-it.title: do they miss it
concept:do-they-miss-it.definition: The startup test: if users would miss the product when it is gone, it is working. The people who set the roadmap have to use the product themselves.

concept:open-source-means-nobody-can-loc.title: open source means nobody can lock you in
concept:open-source-means-nobody-can-loc.definition: Open source is a copyright licence granting copying, use and change. Its real power is that nobody can lock you in. Security depends on whether somebody had the time and money to review the code.

concept:inertia-decides.title: inertia decides
concept:inertia-decides.definition: AI is available to incumbents and newcomers alike, so the outcome is decided by where each sits on the evolution axis and how much past success it has to protect.

chapter:gen-zx.title: Gen ZX: who this book is for, and what it is for
chapter:gen-zx.punchline: Two generations, Z entering the workforce and X the subject-matter experts starting companies, often their parents; together Gen ZX, back to the ZX Spectrum; one objective, that by the end you have started a company; and the measure, the companies created.

chapter:lucky-to-be-here.title: You are lucky to be here
chapter:lucky-to-be-here.punchline: Wonder, not fear: you are starting out in the biggest change of your career, while the pieces are still landing. Spoken to both generations.

chapter:everything-is-connected.title: Everything is connected: graphs
chapter:everything-is-connected.punchline: A graph is a network, not a diagram: the detective's board, a map as a graph with positions, graphs of graphs, provenance as a graph, and start anywhere.

chapter:where-do-you-land.title: Where do you land?
chapter:where-do-you-land.punchline: Maps before names, and the first thing to work out is your centre of gravity: explorer, villager or town planner.

chapter:connect-the-dots-backwards.title: Connect the dots backwards
chapter:connect-the-dots-backwards.punchline: Your path only makes sense looking back; learning is a lifelong skill you can finally shape to how you think; read this on paper.

chapter:what-generative-ai-is.title: What generative AI is
chapter:what-generative-ai-is.punchline: AI is a huge bucket; this book is about the kind that generates; how a language model works in plain words, why a better prompt helps, where hallucinations come from, and where Dinis was corrected.

chapter:lenses-roles-and-loops.title: Lenses, roles and loops
chapter:lenses-roles-and-loops.punchline: The second half of the explanation: a prompt is a lens, a role is a model with a description, an agent is a loop with a goal, tools are requests the model sends back, the model remembers nothing, long chats are compressed, so work in focused threads.

chapter:everyone-is-a-developer.title: Everyone who can brief an agent is a developer
chapter:everyone-is-a-developer.punchline: The definition widened, and so did the door; here is what the briefing-only developer still cannot do.

chapter:explorer-coding-and-the-handover.title: Explorer coding, not vibe coding, and the handover
chapter:explorer-coding-and-the-handover.punchline: What people call vibe coding is exploration, and the word should say so: build to find out, then hand it to the people who will make it something others rely on; the founder's way of building, and both halves.

part:getting-the-job.title: Getting the job, or making it

chapter:hired-for-the-workflow.title: Hired for the workflow
chapter:hired-for-the-workflow.punchline: The one competitive advantage in 2026 is running agentic workflows; you are more technical than you think; it starts with the application.

chapter:act-as-the-job-you-want.title: Act as the job you want
chapter:act-as-the-job-you-want.punchline: If you are looking for a job you have time: do the job in public before you have it, make it linkable, put your CV online. The 2018 Be a founder as then and now: act like a founder then, be one now.

chapter:your-own-newsroom.title: Publish, publish, publish: your own newsroom
chapter:your-own-newsroom.punchline: A publishing loop you can copy on day one; small finished pieces; an article behind every answer.

chapter:your-first-workspace.title: Your first workspace
chapter:your-first-workspace.punchline: From a spreadsheet to a folder per person, in an afternoon; drafts never send; and why your agents should not run on your laptop.

chapter:how-to-work-with-agents.title: How to work with agents
chapter:how-to-work-with-agents.punchline: An agent is a session with a focus; the brief is the unit of work; one shared state across voice, chat and phone; and the trap of a rule per mistake.

chapter:direction-and-judgement.title: Direction is the scarce skill
chapter:direction-and-judgement.punchline: When anyone can build, choosing what to build, when to stop, and where a person belongs is what gets paid for; agents decide, people answer.

chapter:facts-and-the-record.title: Facts, evidence and the record
chapter:facts-and-the-record.punchline: Make fact-based decisions, as the cover says: count rather than remember, let the record check you, distrust self-reports.

chapter:be-a-founder.title: Be a founder: the expert founders
chapter:be-a-founder.punchline: Execution just got cheap: the person who spent twenty years inside a problem can now build the first version of the answer themselves, with agents; a third of new US startups have a single founder, and the fastest-growing founders average 45.

chapter:ship-it-and-see-if-they-miss-it.title: Ship it, and see if they miss it
chapter:ship-it-and-see-if-they-miss-it.punchline: Not to plan, not to pitch, not to architect: ship; give it away, and if they do not miss it, try again; the miss-it test applied to your users and to yourself.

chapter:price-it-then-give-it-away.title: Price it, then give it away
chapter:price-it-then-give-it-away.punchline: Free is never free for the other side: set the price first, then the early-access offer; pay after the value, and let what a page was worth set its price.

chapter:sell.title: Sell
chapter:sell.punchline: Selling a service before the product, a marketplace of people, the SaaS buyer's inertia, and due diligence done by sending an agent rather than a spreadsheet.

chapter:fund-it-or-do-not.title: Fund it, or do not
chapter:fund-it-or-do-not.punchline: Profitable before raising; sell founder shares or lend rather than issue; the controllable founder and what investors buy; the company you keep control of.

chapter:the-company-itself.title: The company itself: the UK, Portugal, Lithuania, the European Union
chapter:the-company-itself.punchline: How to actually do it, for real: a limited company in the UK, the case for Lithuania, Portugal and what it costs to run a small company there, the EU and its programmes, the cloud providers and the startup programmes that exist right now; from experience, not advice.

chapter:building-blocks.title: Serverless, for real
chapter:building-blocks.punchline: If it bills you by the hour when nobody is using it, it is not serverless: no servers of yours with logic in them, no database, the file system as the database, a client-side product on static hosting, and a billing model to match; a founder with no servers has nothing to run at three in the morning.

chapter:privacy-by-design.title: Privacy by design: SG/Send, sgit, and the value of constraints
chapter:privacy-by-design.punchline: Data encrypted on the user's device, on a server that cannot read it; zero-knowledge vaults and where the keys live; the constraint that designs the product and what it does not remove (GDPR); European sovereignty as moving the cloud, not the code.

chapter:controlling-your-agent.title: Controlling your agent: RiskMandate
chapter:controlling-your-agent.punchline: Mandate, reach and the gap; hope versus enforcement; code is a liability; secrets never in the chat; learning to hack is still how you learn. A policy beside the prompt; the behaviour policy is the business logic; the ten questions.

chapter:open-source.title: Open source
chapter:open-source.punchline: Nobody can lock you in; the fork next door; your first pull request. Open source is not free: who pays for what your startup runs on.

chapter:shipped-means-the-user-has-it.title: Shipped means the user has it
chapter:shipped-means-the-user-has-it.punchline: Green does not mean live; tests that never run are not tests; go slow to go fast; five people who do not exist.

chapter:graphs-and-your-future-self.title: Graphs, memory and your future self
chapter:graphs-and-your-future-self.punchline: Memory is context management: many memories, fractal, published and shared; maintain knowledge rather than perfect it; keep your work linkable and backed up for the person you will be.

chapter:civic-responsibility.title: Civic responsibility
chapter:civic-responsibility.punchline: To hack means to solve problems; small countries can lead now that everyone can build; sovereignty is the ability to move. The EU and judo for small countries.

chapter:an-agentic-workflow-from-zero.title: An agentic workflow from zero
chapter:an-agentic-workflow-from-zero.punchline: One afternoon, five exercises: from a spreadsheet to a folder per person, and a first agent that works for you.

chapter:your-first-graph.title: Your first graph, built by hand
chapter:your-first-graph.punchline: Nodes, edges as verbs, and a first graph of something you know, after chapter 15 of Fractal Semantic Graphs.

chapter:five-lenses.title: One idea, five lenses
chapter:five-lenses.punchline: Explain one idea of your own choice for a teenager, a musician, a doctor, a football fan and in another language; see the lens, not the magic.

chapter:a-tiny-agent-loop.title: A tiny agent loop
chapter:a-tiny-agent-loop.punchline: A page of code, or a no-code version, that shows the loop and one tool call: do the task, are we done, go round again.

chapter:images-infographics-and-storyboa.title: Images, infographics and storyboards, drawn by code
chapter:images-infographics-and-storyboa.punchline: A storyboard is data; the picture is drawn in the browser; the quote is checked against its source.

chapter:meeting-briefs-and-follow-ups.title: Meeting briefs and follow-ups
chapter:meeting-briefs-and-follow-ups.punchline: A briefing for you, a briefing on who you meet, a follow-up after: the best-prepared person in the room, every time.

chapter:your-own-publishing.title: Your own newsroom and inbox
chapter:your-own-publishing.punchline: Voice memo in, a checked site out; the email workflow replicated: publishing and communication that scale.

chapter:form-your-company.title: Form your company
chapter:form-your-company.punchline: The steps to a limited company in the UK, and the first look at Lithuania and Portugal; what to decide before you register.

chapter:the-credits-and-programmes-2026.title: The credits and programmes, 2026
chapter:the-credits-and-programmes-2026.punchline: The startup cloud credits and programmes as they stand this year (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Anthropic), what each asks for, and how long they last.

chapter:your-first-price-and-first-ten-c.title: Your first price and your first ten customers
chapter:your-first-price-and-first-ten-c.punchline: Set the price, make the early-access offer, ask after the value, and find ten people who would miss it.

chapter:ship-a-serverless-product-in-a-w.title: Ship a serverless product in a weekend
chapter:ship-a-serverless-product-in-a-w.punchline: Static hosting, a vault for the data, chat on a static site, a payment link and no server of yours: the smallest product that a stranger can pay for.

part:how-this-book-was-made.title: How this book was made, and what you made

chapter:how-this-book-was-made.title: How this book was made, and what you made
chapter:how-this-book-was-made.punchline: The repository and the vault, the roles, the articles as briefs, the decisions, the graph, the loop; co-written with Claude, and the ratio shown. The measure: the companies created from it, and how to tell us.

idea:wonder-not-fear.title: The book opens with wonder, not fear and not technologies
idea:wonder-not-fear.statement: The first edition opened with a slide of logos and went too technical too soon; the second opens with wonder and privilege, and the fear is what the reader hears, not where the book starts.
idea:wonder-not-fear.decided_by: Dinis, in You are lucky to be here (the editor records it in the vault, brief task 1)

sources.where: In short; How the first edition started; What goes where
panels 1 to 4

idea:lucky-to-be-here.title: Whoever reads this now is lucky to be here
idea:lucky-to-be-here.statement: Alive, and starting out, in the middle of a transition this big, while the pieces are still landing: that is luck, and the book says so before anything else.
idea:lucky-to-be-here.decided_by: Dinis, in You are lucky to be here

sources.where: You are lucky to be here; The pieces are still landing

idea:nobody-knows.title: Ignore the doom: nobody knows what happens next
idea:nobody-knows.statement: Every transformation came with the warning that this time is different; this one is televised. The hype may crash, as the dot-com did, and the opportunity was real both times.
idea:nobody-knows.decided_by: Dinis, in You are lucky to be here; whether the dot-com crash belongs in the opening is still his question

sources.where: The hype, and maybe the crash
the counter-story to AI burnout

idea:seven-transformations.title: Seven transformations, lived through: the Spectrum, the BBS, the internet, the mobile phone, the cloud, the apps, AI
idea:seven-transformations.statement: Dinis's own history as the evidence that transitions reward the people who get in early and keep learning; each dated, each with its warning at the time.
idea:seven-transformations.notes: The journalist is to write the history, dated and sourced (brief task 5).

sources.where: The transformations I have lived through
the spectrum panel

idea:technology-finally-works-for-you.title: Technology can finally work for you
idea:technology-finally-works-for-you.statement: Gen Z grew up with technology designed to hook them (the attention economy); with agents they can build again, and make technology serve them.
idea:technology-finally-works-for-you.decided_by: Dinis, in You are lucky to be here; the attention-economy evidence is the journalist's to find

sources.where: Technology that did not work for you
a custom interface for each moment

idea:the-handover.title: The deployment gap is a handover, and the prototype is the best brief
idea:the-handover.statement: The step from a prototype to a tool people rely on is not a place to stop but a handover from explorers to villagers and town planners; what someone built for themselves says what they want better than any document.
idea:the-handover.notes: The mistake is to confuse the brief with a product: the reason SaaS was bought was never the features, it was that the thing is maintained, and every non-functional requirement the vendor partly paid for now lands on an application a non-engineer built in an afternoon. People want to build it and hand it over. The future is village and town-planner companies that take the finished brief and run it, paid by consumption, not by the seat; the handover with agents becomes a file move plus a version bump, logged and reviewable. The case: a European bank piloted a Swiss AI startup's tool, decided to build its own, had a basic prototype six months later that could not handle regulation, data management and daily use, and went back to the startup after a year. Not a weak team, but an explorer team asked to be villagers and town planners as well, on a regulated, data-heavy, daily-use tool; the startup had already done that work many times for many clients. McKinsey's State of AI in 2026: 32 percent of respondents had decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could build it in-house with coding agents. idea:mandate-reach-gap.title: Mandate, reach and the gap: hope versus enforcement
idea:mandate-reach-gap.statement: Before you give an agent access, write down what it is for and what it can reach; the gap is the risk; rules in a prompt are hope, rules in a hook or platform are enforcement; behaviour, decision and workflow policies are different things.
idea:mandate-reach-gap.notes: The product in three words: a hive, a memory and a mandate. Ruflo gives the many hands, an sgit vault the memory the client keeps, an Agent Behaviour Policy each role's mandate. In the first proof of concept the same eleven actions went through the policy engine in enforce mode and six were stopped: four denied, two sent to a person. Read through the Agent Behaviour Policy, a desktop is the agent's grant (everything it can reach) and the task is its mandate; the desktop's job is to keep the first close to the second and leave a footprint that can be read afterwards. That gives nine properties, and the design that follows writes one mandate per task before the desktop exists (what it is for, the hosts it may reach, the secrets it may use and for which hosts, the identity, how long), configures the desktop from it so the grant cannot drift past it by accident, and keeps a vault outside every desktop that it can append to and cannot rewrite. The four objects as the article tables them: mandate (elicited from business and user stories, locked under change control), grant or reach (measured, calibrated against logs), delta (reach minus mandate, derived and never authored) and barriers (none, expectation, setting, boundary; only a boundary is a control). The goal of every engagement is the smallest mandate, the smallest reach, the smallest gap. Self-policing is the fallback, not the goal: the value is in the act of creating the policy, which discovers what is actually possible. Reality is the calibrator: the documentation said an agent could not attach a file to an email, and Claude found a way. Anthropic's own words for why a rule in a prompt is hope: CLAUDE.md files are treated 'as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead', and Claude Code's permission rules 'are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model'. Both modes of reaching a model (the API, where we write the whole system prompt, and the apps and Claude Code, where the vendor's prompt comes first) carry the policy as text the model is asked to keep. Hope or enforcement measured the share of a policy resting on hope falling from 97% to 23% with the right design. The one-sentence test for the barrier column: 'A control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include.' Atlassian's Rovo walked through as the shape of enterprise oversharing: nobody's permissions changed, what changed is that everything they already allowed is now one question away, and who the agent runs as (the person asking, the automation's connection account, or the agent's own account) decides the grant. The Northstar refund as why a behaviour policy is not enough: allowed to refund up to $200, owed $120, paid $150, and every control passes; a decision policy and a workflow policy answer 'who decides' and 'in what order'. The Northstar figures are a scripted simulation, no model called.

idea:the-fork-next-door.title: Open source means nobody can lock you in: the fork next door
idea:the-fork-next-door.statement: Anyone can fork, which protects founders, customers and investors from each other; forks take hold only when someone stops executing; six misconceptions; open source is about to become the most secure software.
idea:the-fork-next-door.notes: The fork as the investor's insurance in place of control: 'A competitor who forks our code today gets our position as of today. They do not get our velocity.' Two conditions make it real: a genuinely open licence, not open core, and a copyright structure not gathered in one corporate holder (every catalogued relicensing between 2018 and 2024 was by a single corporate copyright holder). The fork disciplines the founder because it is possible and protects the founder because it is slow. Relicensing has a pattern: HashiCorp, Elastic and Redis each moved from an open licence to a source-available one, each produced a well-funded fork backed by the cloud providers it targeted (OpenTofu, OpenSearch, Valkey), and two of the three have since added an open licence back. Docker Desktop's paid tier for larger companies (August 2021) worked commercially, with annual recurring revenue past $50 million within months, and the alternatives grew: OrbStack, Colima, Podman Desktop and Rancher Desktop together are about 47% of the five tools' installs through Homebrew over the past year, a figure the article says overstates them. The buyer's side of the same protection: if the only people who can fix a tool are one partner's engineers, the company has swapped a deployment gap for a dependency. With the code open and the record kept, 'who will fix it?' has many answers: your team, the partner, another partner, or the agents, under a mandate, reading the record. Dinis declares a stake: his companies sell open source.

idea:lego-blocks.title: Building blocks: cloud as Lego, free models with your own key, git as a standard
idea:lego-blocks.statement: What a non-specialist can assemble today, mostly free, with an agent doing the one-time setup; serverless as ephemeral town planner services; knowing what tokens cost.
idea:lego-blocks.notes: Costs for a newcomer is still a gap. The four properties serverless always meant to Dinis: it scales to zero, it costs little or nothing when it is not there, it starts fast, and it turns a capability into a commodity. The three words of the name each cover a part the others miss: ephemeral (comes and goes with use, costs nothing when gone), town planner (Wardley's word: mature, industrialised, a commodity, not a prototype held together behind the scenes), services (exposed for others to use, usually through the web). Lambda is an ephemeral town planner service sitting on town planner services like S3, which are always there. The name is a proposal; Dinis does not expect it to replace serverless. The free limits as Cloudflare's pages gave them on 18 October 2026 (they change): static assets free and unlimited on every plan; Workers 100,000 requests a day and 10 ms of CPU each, $5 a month for 10 million; R2 10 GB, a million writes and ten million reads a month, no egress fees, buckets pinnable to the EU; D1 5 GB; KV 100,000 reads and 1,000 writes a day; Durable Objects 100,000 requests a day and 5 GB; Workers AI 10,000 neurons a day then $0.011 per 1,000, 71 models on Cloudflare's own GPUs with a promise not to train on what you send; Email Routing free and unlimited; Access free to 50 users; domains at the registry's price. If staying inside is the point, the model name is the control: a @cf/ model stays on Cloudflare's GPUs, anything else leaves through AI Gateway. The catch for a non-specialist is setup, because Cloudflare's API cannot be called from a web page: a Deploy to Cloudflare button, a temporary account (live for an hour, since June), or an agent with the command line, once. Five packages, each the smallest set for one job and each on the free plan: a site on my domain; my vault, hosted; an assistant over my documents; an inbox that does things; a form or a small API. Each is a repository with a button, a skill and a page saying exactly what it can reach, which is its behaviour policy. The command line is changing: cf entered open beta on 28 September and will replace Wrangler, maintained for 18 months after the beta ends.

It can be held together with tape; nobody using it cares how it was built. Getting it into a stranger's hands is still genuinely hard in 2026, and solving that is the first real product you build. The cost of speed, stated: when the newsroom moved to its own domain, 51 of the 527 figures in its articles did not come with it, and nothing failed in a way a server would have noticed, because the pages were files and they served. The synthetic readers found it. Files make releases cheap and also make it easy to ship something incomplete, which is why every release ends by checking what is actually live.

idea:hack-your-country.title: Civic responsibility: to hack means to solve problems, and small countries can lead now
idea:hack-your-country.statement: Dinis's Portugal talks as the then-and-now: what regulation delivered, the Portuguese Hacking Service, judo for small countries, sovereignty as the ability to move.
idea:hack-your-country.notes: Portuguese edition or both languages is Dinis's open question. Sovereignty as the ability to move, in its practical form: what stops workloads moving is code, not policy or price, and a twin that the application cannot tell from the real service makes the destination a setting. AWS's European Sovereign Cloud went live on 15 January 2026 (first region in Brandenburg, operated by EU residents, 'zero operational control outside of EU borders'), and the article's reading is that sovereignty which depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission. There is no sovereignty without open source and open schemas, because sovereignty means you can leave; the judo move for an operator in Romania, Portugal or the UK is to use the customer's existing code, the hyperscaler's own API and open source as the weight rather than fight them. The word is facilitate, an embassy's job, and the SGraph Send Ambassador role was written to work the way an embassy works: represent, promote trade, build relationships, never hard sales, 'to create the conditions for that organic growth'. The judo playbook in five moves: map the attrition, commoditise the plumbing, create the demand, put the money where the market is still genesis, regulate what settled, then map again, each move using the weight of the larger players rather than matching it. Europe's advantage is strongest in its smaller countries, which can change faster. The article says it is not a national strategy but a map and a set of moves from one person's experience.

idea:reality-corrects-the-graph.statement: A model's first reading of anything will be partly wrong; the plan does not need it right. It needs layers someone knows and predictions something can check: users confirm the top, experts their own layer, tests the execution, and every correction is a commit with a name on it. idea:reality-corrects-the-graph.notes: 'Replicate reality first, then have a fact-based conversation': derive what a parser can derive, deterministically, with a file and a line for every node; let a model propose what a parser cannot see and mark every proposal as proposed; then confront the graph with users, experts and tests. The order for anything built now: brief, plan, architecture, review of the architecture, simulation with synthetic users, code last; the review is the join between the projected graph and the derived one, with three outcomes (match, derived not projected, projected not derived).

idea:a-company-in-the-review.title: There is a company in this: a code review that reads every layer, for somebody to build
idea:a-company-in-the-review.statement: Say the business plainly: a review attached to a repository that keeps the layered graph current per commit and shows each change at every altitude, sold to anyone generating code faster than they can review it, and to teams whose threat model and component layer should be the same graph. What is defensible is the record and the loop, not the model; the scripts are Apache-2.0 and a founder needs a second language and a first customer, not permission.
idea:a-company-in-the-review.notes: One of the business plans published for founders on sgit.ai; an example of the book's advice to start a company from a published plan. The business model settled by the layers: they are the customer's, so the loop runs where the code is, and a company that locked customers into its layers would be selling the one thing it has no right to own. Sell the customised deployment, the running of the loop and the versioned record; give away the grammar, the parser (a commodity) and the model (somebody else's). The offer in one line, from open-source.sgit.ai: 'You can take it. It will cost you that. Or you can pay me, and have it next week.' Who to sell it to: not developers, who have just been told they do not need review, but the people who buy, invest in and acquire software, as due diligence; every vendor that receives the agent has a reason to run it on itself first, which is how review gets back to the developers. 'What differs is the first customer, and the first customer decides whether a company exists.'

idea:the-voice-is-four-inputs.title: The voice is not a setting: a corpus, a memo, a short list of rules, and a reader who corrects
idea:the-voice-is-four-inputs.statement: An agent sounds like its author because of four inputs: a corpus of the author's writing that defines the vocabulary; voice memos that carry how the author thinks, in the order they thought it; a short list of wording rules, each learned from one correction; and the author reading everything before and after it goes live. Take any one away and it stops working. The method transfers; the voice does not.

idea:memory-is-context-management.title: Memory is not a spectator sport: it is context management, many memories, fractal, published and shared
idea:memory-is-context-management.statement: The industry's picture is one store everything is pumped into and retrieved from by similarity. Dinis's is the opposite: memory is deciding what an agent needs in its window now, and no more, because context costs tokens and attention; it is many memories, each with its own vocabulary; it is fractal, principles in a few kilobytes at the top and code at the bottom; it is published and open so an agent can fetch, quote and cite; and it is shared through vaults so a session can end and the next picks up from the same files. The field arrived at files too: a plain filesystem beat a graph memory on the benchmark.

idea:the-file-system-is-the-database.statement: A database server is a large, stateful, always-on thing to provision, secure, back up and pay for, and most of what it holds would be happy as files. LETS loads state, works on it and saves every stage back as files you can version, diff and read: a cache, a database and an audit trail in one, with git as its history. idea:no-server-by-design.title: No server, by design: retire the back end too, and keep only commodity servers
idea:no-server-by-design.statement: After the database, the back end: the newsroom's personas, reading meter, payments, versions and databases all run in the browser, and what is left on the server side is a product someone else runs (static hosting, a vault server that stores only ciphertext, a payment link, DNS, a build pipeline). A constraint did the design: the vault server cannot read anything, so the logic had to go where the key is. It scales without its complexity scaling, ships fast (114 releases in eleven days), and lines up with sovereignty, privacy, explainability and determinism. The one real limit: a secret the reader must not hold cannot live in their browser.
idea:no-server-by-design.notes: Answers the 2018 outline Serverless ('the path to Serverless', 'important to understand the limitations') from the other side: not Lambda, no back end at all. Not a claim that servers are bad: a trading system or a bank's ledger needs shared, live, authoritative state. The August 2026 precedent for the pattern, on sgit.ai: a static site on GitHub Pages has no server, no session and no place to keep a secret, so a chat box could not hold an API key; the answer was three tiers (a local matcher, the reader's own key, a vault bridge), with only the first free. The one real limit (a secret the reader must not hold cannot live in their browser) was met first here. The one real limit met by a product: a capped key per paying user is a secret the user may hold, and the provider's terms, not the architecture, are what stop it. Route 4, a metering proxy, is the smallest possible backend and still a backend: the audio passes through it, so custody, governance, scaling and on-call return and the privacy sentence on the home page has to change. It is also the only route that needs nobody's permission. The same constraint seen from sgit's side: a server that cannot read the data cannot do anything with it, so there is no server code, no deployment and nothing to patch; sgit's server is 'a dumb key-value blob store' and the deployment is the client. Features came from solving the problems the constraint created: clone --path holds only the folders you ask for and carries the rest by id, and with immutable encrypted objects a read is a plain GET, so any static host can serve a vault. Dinis names the temptation he has fallen for himself: a developer makes a change in the cheapest place with the fewest moving parts, which looks like the server until you have to maintain it. The list is the argument: a content site for several audiences where each part runs in the browser (personas opened from a published read key, a meter that charges by the share read and never blocks, a rating that sets the price, a newsroom of your own, SQL and SPARQL over the site's own data), with a 5 pound Stripe payment link and sign-in rented from companies whose product they are, and no account database, no session store, no API server. The lineage is local-first software (Ink and Switch, 2019: you should own your data in spite of the cloud); what vaults add is shared, persistent storage the operator cannot read, so client-side does not have to mean single-device. Next: a model in the client with the reader's own key, personas that follow the reader to every device, a signed receipt for payments, and the architecture packaged as a template another content site can start from. This last is what the weekend chapter would hand a founder.

Security judgement is asking who you are protecting against, accepting what does not match the threat, and naming the condition that would make the gaps unacceptable.

idea:open-source-removes-the-moat-excuse.title: Open source is why it is easy to throw your own technology away
idea:open-source-removes-the-moat-excuse.statement: When everything you build is open, there is no moat you have to keep using and no part of the stack to protect from replacement; you can be the first to replace what you wrote when something better appears. The habit is to ask of every component whether it still earns its place, and open source removes the one bad reason to say yes: that you built it.
idea:open-source-removes-the-moat-excuse.notes: Five reasons that each stand alone: the technology is not the moat, and treating it as open forces you to find what is; code written to be read by strangers has cleaner boundaries; you stay comfortable throwing things away, because a team that has never deleted a component will defend one too long; it is better for the customer, who can read the thing instead of trusting a promise; and it is a better exit for the founder, who leaves with their tools instead of a pile of technology they cannot take. 'Open source is a strategy, not a charity.'

idea:price-it-before-you-give-it-away.title: The four moves after 'do they miss it': define it, price it, deliver it at a flat marginal cost, offer it free to the people who know you
idea:price-it-before-you-give-it-away.statement: Something is not a product until it has a shape, a price and a way of being delivered that does not break you on the tenth customer. Define the thing somebody receives, not the technology. Price it at a number you would be content to be paid, not one from a competitor's page: RiskMandate's ladder is £10 for the pack, £50 for a working vault, £500 for the vault corrected for your situation, £1,500 with two sessions and a professional's signature. Deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time, which the agentic workflow now allows (the twentieth customer costs close to the second). Then give the £500 tier away, twenty of them, to early adopters, power users and past customers, and watch whether they take it at zero. If friendlies will not take it free, a bigger audience will not take it either.
idea:price-it-before-you-give-it-away.notes: Prices as published on 2 October 2026; the early access page went live on 30 September 2026, invite only, and does not say the price. The two outcomes are both in the article: take it and ask for more, and the question becomes price; interesting but no time, does not fit the team, hard to deploy, and the problem is not the price, back to the drawing board.

sources.where: The step after 'do they miss it'; What the programme is, as published; What brutal means

idea:free-is-never-free-for-the-other-si.title: Free is never free for the other side: measure the cost you place on them, then cut it
idea:free-is-never-free-for-the-other-si.statement: Giving something away is not a zero-cost offer. The other side still has to read the message, think about whether it applies, weigh it against their list, find twenty minutes for the prompts and half an hour for a call, and fit a new thing into a team. A price can even help, because it says you are serious. Either way the attrition you place on them is the first thing to measure (time to first reply, who never replied, who started and stopped, what they asked that the message should have answered) and then the thing to cut, until the service costs you the least to provide and costs them the least to receive: no second tool, no account, no overhead on deployment. A commercial product is one people take when the only cost is their own attention.
idea:free-is-never-free-for-the-other-si.notes: Dinis's headline line for this article in Gen ZX Developers. The memo was careful not to make it sound like a lecture, and the book should keep that.

sources.where: Free is not zero; What brutal means

idea:do-not-make-them-apply.title: Do not make them apply: 'we have twenty, would you like one, or shall I give it to someone else'
idea:do-not-make-them-apply.statement: 'Apply for a chance to be considered' asks for work before there is anything in hand and inverts the relationship: they are doing you a favour by using the thing. Say what it is in one sentence, that there are twenty in this round, that they are getting one because they were early, and ask yes or no. Give the first round to the people who paid for something before it was finished; it is a thank-you that is also the best test group, because they know enough to say where it is wrong, and their silence means the most.

sources.where: How to offer it; For the agents running this, steps 1 and 2

idea:count-created-customised-used.title: Count what matters: created, customised, used, and the minutes it cost the other side; set the stop rule first
idea:count-created-customised-used.statement: For an early access programme the numbers are: how many were created, how many customised, how many used, how many runs; a thing created and never customised is a download, customised and never used is a document, and the commercial value is in the third number. Add corrections received, the strongest sign someone read it, and the minutes each step cost the person on the other side and where they stopped. Every stop is a product change to make, not a reason the customer gave. Set the stop rule before the first message goes out: if, after the first twenty, fewer than a handful ran it and sent a correction, the programme stops and the drawing board starts.
idea:count-created-customised-used.notes: In the article the counts are RiskMandate's (Agent Behaviour Policies created, customised, used, scenarios run); the book generalises the shape. The programme records timestamps and steps only, no message content.

sources.where: What we count; For the agents running this, steps 3 to 6

idea:pay-after-the-value.title: Pay after the value: credit first, a meter, a balance that can go below zero, and no subscription by default
idea:pay-after-the-value.statement: Most purchases are bets on future value, and the bet is often lost: gym members on a flat fee of over $70 attended 4.3 times a month and paid more than $17 a visit when a $10-a-visit pass was on offer. Turn it round where you can: start the user with credit, charge for the share they actually use, let the balance go negative, and ask for payment when the value is in view. A subscription is a discount for regular use, not rent on something somebody ignores; do not reach for one by default. The condition is a very large gap between the cost of serving and what you can charge, which a static site on a CDN has in the extreme and a business with a real cost per unit does not. Make it fair by country, visible in where the money goes, and chosen at more than one level.
idea:pay-after-the-value.notes: The newsroom's meter: everyone starts with £5.00 of credit; 10p for a new article read to the end, 5p for an older one, only as far as read; the balance can go below zero and nothing is blocked. The article says there are no results yet and the review is on 6 December 2026; the gym, theatre and photo studies explain the psychology, not the newsroom's results. The reader (read/) on this site runs by the same rules.

sources.where: Buying the future; The newsroom's version; Where it works; Fair, visible, chosen

idea:profitable-before-raising.title: Fund it, or do not: the worst time to raise is before you are profitable, and the best is when they call you
idea:profitable-before-raising.statement: Raising before the product, before the fit and before profit means bargaining from weakness with a clock running, and the worst terms are not about money but control: a say in the business handed to people whose job is a return, not the mission. Profitability means time, and being able to wait is most of a negotiating position. Do not get signed before you have the album. With agents making execution cheap, getting to that position before you need anyone's money is more possible than it has ever been; then the choice of investor is yours. Not never raise: raise from strength, on terms you set, from people who came to you because the thing already works.
idea:profitable-before-raising.notes: The chapter's centre, which the register lacked as its own node. The article's caveat on price: it might not be profitable today and still be right if the economics improve with scale, but keep the gap small enough to self-fund.

idea:we-study-survivors.title: We study survivors: a risky practice can look like the cause of success when only winners are counted
idea:we-study-survivors.statement: Business writing looks at the winners, lists what they did, and says do the same; it almost never counts the people who did exactly the same and failed, or were never funded. Denrell showed in 2003 that risky practices unrelated to performance across everyone can look positively related to it in a sample of survivors. So the question is not what the winners did but why that one was chosen, funded and backed when others who did the same were not. Timing and place matter too: in MusicLab, showing popularity made success more unequal and less predictable, and the ten largest computer-science clusters hold 69% of US inventors in the field.
idea:we-study-survivors.notes: Also the reader's defence against the book's own founder stories. Denrell, Vicarious Learning, Undersampling of Failure, and the Myths of Management, Organization Science, 2003; Salganik, Dodds and Watts, Science, 2006; Moretti, AER, 2021.

sources.where: The survivors we study; Luck, place and timing

idea:investors-select-for-control.title: Investors select for the founder they can steer; control is written into the contract, and founders get replaced
idea:investors-select-for-control.statement: Dinis's hypothesis: between two founders with the same idea, drive and talent, one deciding factor is which one the investor believes they can control. The nearest tested trait is coachability, which investors openly prefer though 'being coachable doesn't necessarily make your firm more successful'. Control is in the paperwork: Kaplan and Strömberg found that when a firm performs poorly the investors obtain full control, and only when it performs very well do they give most of it back; non-compete and vesting terms make leaving expensive. Wasserman found 50% of founders no longer CEO by year three and fewer than 25% leading the IPO. The investors' answer is that control creates value (each level of founder control cut pre-money valuation by 17.1 to 22.0 percent), but that measures exits, not the mission; founder-led companies in the S&P 500 performed 3.1 times better in shareholder returns from 1990 to 2014. In Wardley terms the investor moves the founder towards commodity, as record labels did to performers once the songs, the producers and the distribution were the assets.
idea:investors-select-for-control.notes: The article's own limits: no study tests controllability directly; the value evidence cuts against the argument; Bain's figures are not peer-reviewed; the founder-tenure figures are from the late 1990s and early 2000s; not that investors are villains; and Dinis has a stake. The profile it says is filtered out is the founder with a strong vision and strong ethics, which it says is close to many European founders.

sources.where: Who is the commodity; Why one and not the other; Control is written into the contract; Founders get replaced; The investors' answer, and the long run

idea:sell-dont-issue.title: Sell, don't issue: the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and nobody buys the steering wheel
idea:sell-dont-issue.statement: For a founder who has already won (paying customers, profit, growth, more than one investor who wants in): instead of the company issuing new shares, the investor buys ordinary shares the founder already owns, in a private sale, so the founder is paid now for years of underpaid work, the company is not diluted, and no board seat, veto or liquidation preference comes with the money. If the company needs cash, the founder lends part of the proceeds back, subordinated by contract to every other creditor, at a modest fixed rate or none, repaid if the company succeeds. A founder lending their own money watches every penny, and 74% of high-growth internet startups fail from premature scaling. The investor's insurance is not control but the fork: with everything open source, if the founder goes wrong they can take the code and back a better service.
idea:sell-dont-issue.notes: The worked example, illustrative: a UK company worth £10 million, £2 million invested, the founder keeps 80% either way; in the sale the founder pays about £420,000 in tax (18% on the first £1 million under Business Asset Disposal Relief from 6 April 2026, 24% above) and has about £1.58 million, lends £0.75 million and keeps about £0.83 million; the buyer pays 0.5% stamp duty. The article says no study tests the model, the fork as insurance is an argument not a tested mechanism, it is not tax or legal advice, and Dinis has a stake. The fork is slow both ways: three months at best, closer to a year, for an established company to reach where the original team is.

sources.where: Sell, don't issue; Lend, don't dilute; The open source safety valve; Why it could raise the odds; A worked example

idea:what-breaks-when-you-sell-not-issue.title: What breaks: EIS is lost on bought shares, a big early sale reads as doubt, the founder-lender is a creditor, and a broad non-compete closes the fork
idea:what-breaks-when-you-sell-not-issue.statement: The model has costs a founder should know before the term sheet does. UK angels get EIS relief of 30% and SEIS of 50% only on newly issued shares, so bought shares are that much dearer to them; expect a lower price or a hybrid with some new shares. Common stock is often priced 10% to 30% below the last round. Balderton says it would not expect a founder to sell more than 10% at growth stage and has walked away over the size of a secondary. A founder who sells and lends back has moved part of their risk ahead of the new investors unless the loan is subordinated in writing. Control can return through a shareholders' agreement, and the model only holds if the founder refuses those terms. And refuse a broad non-compete: it keeps the fork for the investors and takes it from the founder; offer confidentiality, no poaching and no use of the brand instead.
idea:what-breaks-when-you-sell-not-issue.notes: Fits badly: deep tech, hardware, a land grab against funded rivals, proprietary code (no fork), investors whose model needs control rights. The UK figures are for 2026/27; the EY secondary pricing data is from Indian deals; the UK's 2023 plan to cap non-competes at three months was never legislated. Four fine-print points for a lawyer are in the article: transfer restrictions, selling above market value as employment income, success-linked interest treated as a distribution, and the order of issue and sale in a hybrid.

sources.where: What breaks; When it works and when it does not

idea:the-expert-founders-in-numbers.title: The expert founders, in numbers: 45 is the mean age, experience doubles the odds, a third of US startups have one founder
idea:the-expert-founders-in-numbers.statement: In a study of 2.7 million US founders the mean age at founding of the 1-in-1,000 fastest-growing new ventures is 45.0, and founders with three or more years in the same industry reached top-tier growth at twice the rate of those with none. Carta: solo founders rose from 23.7% of new US startups in 2019 to 36.3% in the first half of 2025. Stripe: its top 100 AI companies reached $1 million in annualised revenue in a median of 11.5 months. The venture model behind the outsider playbook: in Horsley Bridge's data on just over 7,000 investments from 1985 to 2014, about half returned less than the original investment and 6% of deals produced 60% of total returns. The experts were never held back by knowledge; they were held back by access to capital, engineers and the long build before anything could be shown, which is the part that got cheap.
idea:the-expert-founders-in-numbers.notes: The article says the AI growth figures are the fastest, not the typical, and some are the promoter's own. Azoulay, Jones, Kim and Miranda, Age and High-Growth Entrepreneurship, AER: Insights, 2020. Dinis's Gen ZX article repeats the 45 and the one-third in its 'Precisely' section.

sources.where: The playbook that worked; Execution just got cheap; The experts were always the better bet

idea:europe-suits-the-expert-founder.title: Europe's slower, sceptical money suits a founder who can build first
idea:europe-suits-the-expert-founder.statement: European investors are said to want to see it working, and the data has a version of it: European companies raise at higher revenue (a median band of $1 million to $5 million against $100,000 to $1 million in the US), at lower pre-money valuations ($6.54 million against $14.64 million), with funding targets 46% smaller. That scepticism is what an expert founder now needs, because money too soon is one of the worst things that can happen: 74% of high-growth internet startups fail from premature scaling and investors put in 2 to 3 times more than needed in the discovery phase. Europe is weak at scaling (5% of global VC funds raised against 52% in the US; close to 30% of unicorns founded in Europe 2008 to 2021 moved abroad), and strong at the first part, which is the part that now matters most. Its values fit too: an open source strategy in the Commission's June 2026 sovereignty package, and impact at 15% of European VC against 7% in North America.
idea:europe-suits-the-expert-founder.notes: The article calls the Europe and US comparison weakly evidenced: one vendor's aggregated data (Equidam), no clean Series A study. Could also serve the-company-itself (the EU) or civic-responsibility (judo for small countries); placed with funding because the argument is about when money arrives.

sources.where: Why this favours Europe

idea:sg-send-live-in-five-days.title: SG/Send: first commit on 8 February, live on 13 February, Stripe on 1 March, ten paying customers on 2 March, a feature request shipped in 90 minutes
idea:sg-send-live-in-five-days.statement: The first commit was on 8 February 2026, with a spec that set the rule everything since has followed: files encrypted on the client, the key never sent. send.sgraph.ai was live on 13 February. The Stripe checkout went live on 1 March; on 2 March there were ten paying customers, recruited with an offer of £5 of credits and a £5 Amazon voucher, which several declined. The first feature request, a folder not a file, came the same day and was proposed at 20:26, implemented at 20:48 and given a viewer at 22:15. Taking it to market end to end is where Dinis learnt Stripe, pricing and the rest a real product needs, which paid off later in the newsroom.
idea:sg-send-live-in-five-days.notes: Dated story for the chapter and for your-first-price-and-first-ten-customers. The article says '30 paying customers' appears only in an investor one-pager and could not be verified; ten is the recorded number. Every date and quote was checked in the repositories by two research agents.

idea:silence-is-a-signal.title: The technology worked and the use case did not: 'users buy credits, test once, and don't come back'
idea:silence-is-a-signal.statement: SG/Send's briefs said it on 5 March 2026, three days after the first ten customers: paying customers but not enough usage, credits sitting unused. Nobody ran out of credits and came back for more, and nobody came back asking for the next feature; that silence was the signal. It was a platform without a workflow that needed it. The same features are used now because the newsroom, RiskMandate and the vaults need them: explorers find things early, and the use case decides when they matter. The miss-it test, failed, in numbers.
idea:silence-is-a-signal.notes: Usage is described, not counted: the article found no usage figures. The pace behind it: 4,476 commits on 246 of the first 249 days, 739 release tags from v0.1.0 to v0.34.0; the command line's unit tests grew from 237 on 5 March to 4,232 on 14 October.

idea:the-agents-wrote-the-code-i-wrote-t.title: The agents wrote the code, Dinis wrote the briefs and merged: 38% of commits in February, over 85% from September
idea:the-agents-wrote-the-code-i-wrote-t.statement: Of the 1,671 commits under Dinis's name on the SG/Send app, 1,298 are merges of the agents' branches and most of the rest are brief files. The agents' share of the app's commits rose from 38% in February 2026 to over 85% from September. The way of working was written down on the day the site went live: voice memos become briefs, briefs flow down, debriefs flow up; explorers and villagers from 14 February, no town planners yet.

idea:decided-by-inertia-not-by-ai.title: The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI, because AI is available to both sides
idea:decided-by-inertia-not-by-ai.statement: The incumbents have the same models the newcomers have, plus more data, more engineers and more money; if the technology decided this they would already have won, and two and a half years in they have not. What decides it is where a company sits on the evolution axis and how much past success it has to protect: Nokia met the mobile phone with nothing to protect and became the category, met the iPhone with fifteen years of success to protect and was gone from it within seven. Past success breeds inertia; new entrants, unencumbered by it, initiate the change. The newcomer was never on the rails, which is why the newcomers, not the incumbents, are the ones to watch.
idea:decided-by-inertia-not-by-ai.notes: The February 2026 'SaaSpocalypse': roughly $285 billion left the sector in about 48 hours after Anthropic shipped Cowork plug-ins, and the market recovered by September with the argument that the database is the moat; the article reads that recovery as 'the apocalypse, priced'. The claim is stated 'so it can be wrong'.
