idea:users-were-never-happy.title: Users were never happy: 91% frustrated, 80% of features rarely or never used, $21 million a year in idle licences
idea:users-were-never-happy.statement: Business software did 80% of what you needed and the remaining 20% was as painful as before you bought it, and it is measured: Freshworks found 91% of 8,698 people frustrated by inadequate workplace technology; Pendo found 80% of features in the average product rarely or never used, across 615 products; Zylo puts the average organisation's waste on unused licences at $21 million a year. 73% of companies prepare VAT returns in Excel and 78% of British companies say spreadsheets support key financial decisions: the persistence of Excel is the clearest evidence that SaaS failed them, because it is the one tool where they control the shape of the thing. You pay 100% for the 10% of features you actually wanted.
idea:users-were-never-happy.notes: The article rejects the famous Standish 64% (a 2002 keynote based on four internal applications) in favour of Pendo's sample. Why a founder's opening is in old, unloved software.

sources.where: First, the part nobody likes to say: users were never happy

idea:what-they-refused-to-build-is-what-.title: What SaaS refused to build to protect its moat is exactly what a customer's agent needs
idea:what-they-refused-to-build-is-what-.statement: Portability, open schemas, a real API at the centre, data you can take out, capabilities you can call from outside: for twenty years these were treated as churn risks and starved. Now the customer's agent turns up wanting exactly that list and finds a product built to prevent it; the moat has become the thing the water cannot get past in either direction. Strip the interface and most of these companies are a database, a messaging system and a state machine, and that can be built, though it is hard to build well. A founder builds the list from the start.
idea:what-they-refused-to-build-is-what-.notes: Pairs with the-fork-next-door and open-source-removes-the-moat-excuse: the newcomer's version of not having a moat to protect.

sources.where: The irony, which is the whole article in one paragraph; Strip the UI and see what is left

idea:the-company-sits-in-the-two-moves.title: A company sits in the two moves on the map: a guess becoming a product, and a product becoming a commodity
idea:the-company-sits-in-the-two-moves.statement: Who reads the code depends on where it is on the map: explorer code is read for intent, mostly by agents; villager code is read line by line, because this is where changes land and the blast radius lives; town planner code is read by deterministic checks at the boundary, with a person for the exceptions. The company sits in the two moves between them: from explorer to villager, when a guess becomes a product and needs the review it never had; from villager to town planner, when a product becomes a commodity and the review becomes checks that run without anyone. The trap on both sides is not knowing which stage the code is at: teams find a model's mistakes too risky and swing to reviewing everything by hand.
idea:the-company-sits-in-the-two-moves.notes: Quote, word for word, from the March 2026 article the newsroom cites: 'Before AI agents started writing code, you could argue that 90% of the code running in production was not being read by anyone.' The SaaS article's version: businesses that take the finished brief and run it, paid by consumption and by the fact that it keeps working, not by the seat; and 'more engineers, not fewer'. Extends the-handover from a frame about prototypes to a frame about where a company's value is.

sources.where: Who reads the code; The company
The mistake, and where the money actually is: village and town-planner companies

idea:a-budget-per-step-is-the-objective-.title: A budget per step, declared before anything runs, is the objective way to say good enough; the five whys move it
idea:a-budget-per-step-is-the-objective-.statement: Agents keep going, that is what they do, and one agent handing work to another looks efficient while it spends. The way to stay on the right side of diminishing returns is a budget per altitude and per change, decided in advance, so a workflow's maximum cost is knowable before it runs rather than discovered afterwards; work handed from agent to agent carries its budget and never widens it. Being able to tell a team the budget is spent was one of the most useful controls Dinis ever had, because teams are very good at keeping going. Then the five whys: every finding at one layer is a question about the layer below, and the fix goes there as a rule, so the next change like it is caught for the price of a query. Onboard by starting at one point and continuing, never by analysing everything.
idea:a-budget-per-step-is-the-objective-.notes: The junior's version of knowing-when-to-stop, as a mechanism rather than an experience. Every agent doing the work runs under a behaviour policy written before its first run.

sources.where: From art to science; Constraints keep it in control, the five whys make it cheaper

idea:due-diligence-becomes-an-agent.title: Send an agent, not a spreadsheet: due diligence derived from the code, not composed by the vendor
idea:due-diligence-becomes-an-agent.statement: Due diligence was a form because the alternative did not exist: the standard questionnaire has 627 questions, vendors answer 37.3 requests a month and spend 179 hours on them, and the answers are written by the people being asked. Now a buyer can send a prompt, or a small agent under a behaviour policy, to run inside the vendor's environment and come back with a graph of what is there: what reaches production that no person reviewed, whether the documentation matches the code, whether there is a threat model, what the last fifty bugs touched, which agents touch the pipeline and under what policy. The vendor reads what leaves and can redact but not rewrite, because the answer is derived, and companies will not put a false map on a record. A buyer asking costs nothing; a supplier not answering looks worse than one answering badly. Investors and acquirers get the same visibility in the same month.
idea:due-diligence-becomes-an-agent.notes: The agent does not exist yet; the article is the case for it. The regulation arrives before the visibility: the EU Product Liability Directive applies to products placed on the market from 9 December 2026 and presumes a product defective where the manufacturer fails to disclose relevant evidence. Placed in sell because it is what the founder's buyers will do to them.

sources.where: The form that never connected to anything; What changed; The consequence that has been missing

idea:double-down-on-understandability.title: A startup should double down on understandability: less code, the same tools, and it can be checked and pass
idea:double-down-on-understandability.statement: The test is risk-based, not pure. A startup that says it generated most of its code fast, that the product is not mission-critical and here are the mitigations has passed; what fails is not knowing. So build the graph of your own repository, keep the threat model with the code, write a behaviour policy for every agent, trace bugs to changes, and answer the buyer's questions in the buyer's format before being asked. The startup can play the same game as the biggest buyer, with open source tools, and it has less code: understanding ten thousand lines is a week, ten million that nobody still at the company wrote is a programme. The incumbent's advantage was that nobody could check; the startup's is that it can be checked and pass.
idea:double-down-on-understandability.notes: A threat model is the fastest read of a team's understanding: one that says 'we have a weakness here, exploiting it needs a nation-state, we will not defend against it' is a good one. The evidence that review is being skipped is dated in the article: AI accounts for 42% of committed code and only 48% always verify it (Sonar, January 2026); 80% of PRs have no human comment when an AI review tool is on (Qodo, 2025).

sources.where: Risk-based, not pure; The consequence that has been missing: 'if I were a startup I would double down on understandability'

idea:the-behaviour-policy-is-the-due-dil.title: The agent behaviour policy is the due diligence document: a buyer reads the blast radius off it, and its absence says the most
idea:the-behaviour-policy-is-the-due-dil.statement: A behaviour policy, written before an agent's first run, says what the agent is, which identity it uses, what it may read, write, not do and spend, who approves what, which risks were accepted by whom and for how long, and where its actions are recorded. Read by a buyer it says something else: the worst case (a deploy agent whose identity has no merge right and no production credential can at most break staging), which controls are enforced by the identity and which are only instructions, and which risks the vendor accepted on the buyer's behalf. A vendor with agents in its pipeline and no policy to show has agents whose blast radius nobody has written down, which is a finding before any code is read.
idea:the-behaviour-policy-is-the-due-dil.notes: Quote worth keeping: 'the moment of authorisation is not when you allow the agent to do something, it is the moment you give them the permissions.' A buyer reads the permissions, not the promises. Extends mandate-reach-gap from the operator's view to the buyer's.

sources.where: The behaviour policy is the due diligence document

idea:the-engagement-path-starts-small.title: Selling a service: each step small enough to say yes to, and each ends with something they keep
idea:the-engagement-path-starts-small.statement: The path for selling an agentic service: a free conversation about what the client wants agents to do and must never do; a first run on a real problem for £10 to £50 that leaves a vault; £500 for about two hours or £1,500 for a day to steer it or write the behaviour policy for one team; a four-day pilot in their own environment for £5,000; then a maintained setup from £149 a month so they run it themselves. The boutique benchmarks are the same shape everywhere: a free call, a paid discovery (a one-week audit at £2,500, a 14-day sprint at €2,900, a two-week assessment at $4,999), a fixed-price pilot (from £8,000), a build, a retainer. The prices are hypotheses to test with the first ten customers, and the plan says so: no paid run yet.
idea:the-engagement-path-starts-small.notes: Prices from ruv.sgit.ai's published offers and the boutiques' public pages, read on 16 October 2026. The market map's positions are a judgement, as the article says.

sources.where: Who else is selling this; The engagement path

idea:evidence-first-is-the-position.title: The market is crowded at the top and thin on evidence: sell the record the client keeps
idea:evidence-first-is-the-position.statement: The large consultancies each have an agent platform, the model vendors sell through partners and their own engineers, and boutiques sell fixed-price pilots; what the people in between lack is not another platform but evidence they can inspect. Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs, unclear value and inadequate risk controls, and warns of agent washing. The position for a small seller is evidence first: every engagement leaves a vault the client keeps, with the work, the history and a ledger of what each agent did and was allowed to do. The demonstration is the sales process, and the demonstration is checkable.
idea:evidence-first-is-the-position.notes: The demonstration: a talk built and run by a governed agent hive in about a day, 28 workers, 57 vault commits, no plaintext in anything the server stored, every vault deleted at the end; the runs were not gated by a compiled behaviour policy, which was shown separately. Dinis proposes 'agentics' as the word for what is sold: the practice, not one workflow.

sources.where: Where the gap is; What we showed

idea:a-marketplace-of-people.title: A service only scales with people: a curated marketplace of consultants, joined by proof of work
idea:a-marketplace-of-people.statement: Agentic engagements need someone who knows the client's world and can steer a hive in it, and there are more of those people in a community than hours in a founder's week. So alongside the offers, a small curated list of consultants who deliver on the same stack, where the client picks the kind of project first and then the people. Joining copies the markets that work: apply, show proof of work (a public vault or repository of a real run with its ledger), peer review by two members, a thirty to forty-five minute interview with a scenario, a first engagement shadowed, and standards including a behaviour policy for consultants, the same idea applied to agents. The consultant sets the price within the band and keeps most of it; markets sit between 5% and 20% in total (Malt charges freelancers 5%, Upwork 0% to 15%, Braintrust 15% to the client).
idea:a-marketplace-of-people.notes: Nothing is built; the platform share is a proposal; the first two consultants (Mondweep Chakravorty and Dinis) are not taking bookings. Toptal says fewer than 3% of applicants pass its five stages. Also a door for the reader going into a job: join as the person who delivers.

sources.where: A marketplace for the people who deliver it; A brief for the marketplace page

idea:three-tiers-for-a-model-on-a-static.title: Three honest tiers for a model on a site with no server: a local matcher, your own key, or a vault bridge
idea:three-tiers-for-a-model-on-a-static.statement: A static site has no server, no session and no place to keep a secret, so the usual chat box (a backend holding the API key) is not an option. The honest choices are three: a deterministic matcher in the browser that is free, private, works offline and shows which words it matched on (the default, because a reader should never have to hold a credential to use an index); the reader's own key, opt-in and labelled, which lives in the page's origin and is a trust decision presented as one; and a vault bridge where the host holds the key below the permission floor and the app never sees it. When the model call fails, fall back to the first tier and say so.
idea:three-tiers-for-a-model-on-a-static.notes: Dated 27 August 2026, with an addendum of 7 September: the pane on every page was given seven tools over the site's own index, and shows every call it made. The bridge's own qualification travels with it, quoted: 'The bridge protects your key; it is not yet a boundary that prevents all egress.' Only the first tier is free; the third was not built (on the board as T11).

sources.where: The constraint nobody can design around; The three tiers

idea:route-do-not-teach.title: Scope the feature to one question, and quote rather than paraphrase
idea:route-do-not-teach.statement: The directory chat answers one question (which of the nineteen sites is mine) and refuses to teach the subjects: the sites already contain the arguments, and a summary that drifts from them is worse than a link that does not. It knows only the catalogue, nineteen theses and summaries quoted from each site's own words. For a founder shipping in a weekend, that is the discipline: the narrow thing that is right over the wide thing that drifts.
idea:route-do-not-teach.notes: Sits next to stale-pages-become-false-memories and disagree-rationally-with-provenance: the same rule (every item carries its source, nothing paraphrased) applied to a product feature. The catalogue is generated from the same data as the cards and the table, which is why it can be trusted.

sources.where: What it does not do

idea:billing-by-not-building-billing.title: Billing by not building billing: the commercial model is a property of the key
idea:billing-by-not-building-billing.statement: A user pays five pounds through a payment link; the company keeps its cut at the moment of payment; the rest becomes the credit limit on a key handed to the user; the provider meters it and the key stops when it is spent. Against a billing system (a meter on every call, a ledger per user, disputes, refunds, fraud, custody of the data while it meters) that is a payment, a cut, a key with a ceiling and nothing else, and it is more profitable per pound because the margin is taken once, up front. The minimum top-up is five pounds because a card fee with a fixed component makes a one-pound purchase return about 59 pence of inference.
idea:billing-by-not-building-billing.notes: Could also sit in price-it-then-give-it-away. The model was written down on 28 July 2026, the day the product started, in a brief headed 'Billing by not building billing'. It is why a router like OpenRouter does well: it sells credit, keeps a margin and meters for everyone else. The user owns the ceiling: a key with a limit cannot cost more than the limit, and the user can revoke it at the provider in one click.

sources.where: The commercial model that was never a billing system

idea:the-licence-is-the-blocker.title: Twice now the product was possible and the licence was the blocker: read the terms, not only the docs
idea:the-licence-is-the-blocker.statement: Every technical piece for renting a Mac to an agent by the minute exists, and Apple's macOS licence forbids leasing a Mac for less than twenty-four consecutive hours, and only for developer services. OpenRouter's Management API documents 'unique API keys for each customer instance' with credit limits, and section 7(4) of its terms (31 August 2026) forbids 'reselling API access to Models', so a plan built against the docs was dead on the page that documented it. Before a founder builds the commercial model on a provider, the terms are the thing to read, and an enterprise or OEM agreement is a door to ask about, not a feature to assume.
idea:the-licence-is-the-blocker.notes: The cost of the licence, from the desktop article, at prices read on 7 October 2026: 44 hours of work a month costs about $7.29 on an E2B or Daytona Linux sandbox, $17.60 on Windows 365 for Agents, 116.16 euros on a Scaleway Mac mini M4, $649.44 on an AWS M4 and $1,040.16 on an M4 Pro, because each day is a 24-hour lease. Quote: 'The Mac is not expensive per hour; it is expensive because the hour you can buy is a day.' Both articles say they are read, not interpreted, and are not legal advice; the book should say the same. The nearest fit found for the capped key was ElevenLabs: per-key credit limits, OEM terms under which a business sets its own price for its end users, and a grants programme (twelve months, for companies under 25 people with a monetised use).

sources.where: the opening; The commercial model that was never a billing system; The four routes
macOS has a one-day minimum, and a purpose clause

idea:voicedebrief-stopped-at-the-billing.title: VoiceDebrief: a product with no server that shipped in three weeks and stopped at the one thing it could not sell
idea:voicedebrief-stopped-at-the-billing.statement: VoiceDebrief.ai turns a voice note into a transcript, a translation and a debrief in the browser, on the user's own OpenRouter key, with no account, no server and nothing stored; a 42-second note costs about a third of a penny. Built in the open from 28 July 2026: 239 commits and 27 releases in the first three weeks, then eleven commits the week after, then three, and a last commit on 7 September. What stopped it was not a server but the lack of one: the capped key per user that the model needed is forbidden by the provider's terms, and the alternative, a metering proxy, is the backend the product exists to avoid.
idea:voicedebrief-stopped-at-the-billing.notes: Dated 12 October 2026; Dinis says he is involved in VoiceDebrief and that the commit counts show when the work stopped, not why. The four routes: buy a capped OpenRouter key per user (forbidden by the standard terms); a provider that sells the capped key itself or lets it be issued under its terms (ElevenLabs the nearest fit, the gap is one sentence); bring your own key, kept (what runs today, honest, no margin, and the five minutes it takes to get a key is where most people stop); a metering proxy (the smallest backend, and a backend, custody and on-call return). The one part of the product with a server is the WhatsApp path, an n8n workflow behind a Cloudflare Worker. The method at the end is worth the book's attention: agents draft the letters to providers, Dinis sends, the ask is one sentence, and every answer is recorded as an issue with its date so the map is updated as a version rather than a new article.

sources.where: What VoiceDebrief is; Why no server is the product; The four routes

idea:git-for-things-you-cannot-put-on-gi.title: Git for things you cannot put on GitHub: what an encrypted vault is
idea:git-for-things-you-cannot-put-on-gi.statement: There is a category of file with nowhere good to live: a risk register with real system names, an analysis still being argued about, the working memory of an agent that has read your codebase for a month, client material under NDA. It wants history, branches, diffs and a link, and it is the reason people say 'we can't put that in GitHub', so it ends up in a shared drive or a thread nobody can diff. sgit is git for those files: encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned like git, stored on a server that holds ciphertext and nothing else, not filenames, not directory structure, not commit messages. There is no key escrow, no admin override and no support engineer who can recover it, which is a feature with a real cost.
idea:git-for-things-you-cannot-put-on-gi.notes: Dated 25 August 2026. The evidence in the article: an object is 786 bytes of AES-256-GCM ciphertext named by the SHA-256 of the encrypted bytes, so the host can deduplicate it, cache it and serve it from a CDN without knowing what it is; all nineteen published vaults cloned from their published keys, 1,389 files, no failures. Underneath it is real version control (multi-parent commits, a tree per directory, merge-base, three-way merge), not a sync folder. Status, plainly: sgit is beta and says so on every page; pip install sgit-ai, pure Python, two runtime dependencies, Apache-2.0. The then-and-now for the 2018 Backup your life: back up into a vault whose key you hold.

sources.where: the opening; The part that is easy to say and hard to build

idea:the-read-key-is-the-sharing-model.title: One string is address, authorisation and key; the read key derived from it is safe to publish
idea:the-read-key-is-the-sharing-model.statement: A vault key is a passphrase and a vault id in one string, and it is three things at once: the address of the vault, the authorisation to write to it, and the key that decrypts it. Lose it and the data is gone; leak it and someone can rewrite your history. From it, one way, comes a read key: same vault, read-only, safe to publish, and the read key is the entire credential, with no account, no login and no access request. That asymmetry is the whole sharing model: every vault linked from sgit.ai is published as a read key, and no vault key has ever been published, a rule enforced by a tripwire in the release pipeline.
idea:the-read-key-is-the-sharing-model.notes: This site runs on the same rule: the public read key in admin/content/vault.json is the only key that belongs in the repository, and the gate refuses the private prefix (CLAUDE.md). The second article adds the other credentials that sit beside the vault key, each made for one job: a write key the server checks as a hash, an append token that writes one message to one lane and nothing else, and a PKI key pair (RSA-OAEP 4096 for encryption, ECDSA P-256 for signing). In the browser the key sits after the # in the URL, which browsers do not send to the server.

sources.where: The part that is easy to say and hard to build; Ten seconds of proof; Try it
One secret, and the keys derived from it

idea:capability-without-credential.title: An app in a vault runs against the vault without ever being handed a key
idea:capability-without-credential.statement: A vault can contain an application, not only documents, and the application runs against the vault without ever holding a credential: it declares permissions of nothing, the host reads the vault and passes results in, and the app never sees a key. Capability without credential means you can run code you did not write against data you care about, with the blast radius set by a config file you can read in one screen. The same shape holds for a model: the key lives below the permission floor, the host makes the call, and the app never sees it.
idea:capability-without-credential.notes: Belongs beside mandate-reach-gap: the config file is the written reach, enforced by the host rather than hoped for in a prompt. The chat article's qualification applies: the bridge protects the key it was trusted with; it does not yet stop a malicious app calling a provider with a credential of its own.

sources.where: The part that surprises people
Tier 2, the bridge

idea:protect-the-keys-not-the-data.title: Encryption on the client moves the problem from the data to the keys, and the sovereignty line to whoever holds them
idea:protect-the-keys-not-the-data.statement: When the server can read what it stores, all of it has to be protected: every copy, backup, log and replica, and every person and process with access. When the server holds ciphertext named by the hash of that ciphertext, the problem moves to protecting the keys, which is much smaller, and the key becomes the whole question: where it is kept and how it travels decides who can read, who can write and what a leak costs. The sovereignty line stops being where the data is stored and becomes who holds the keys, so data can sit with a provider or in a country with sovereignty gaps and you remain sovereign over it and able to move it; the European Data Protection Board treats strong encryption with the keys retained solely by the exporter as an effective supplementary measure for transfers.
idea:protect-the-keys-not-the-data.notes: The EDPB source is Recommendations 01/2020, version 2.0, 18 June 2021, use case 1, quoted in the article: 'the EDPB considers that the encryption performed provides an effective supplementary measure.' The same idea as sovereignty as the ability to move (hack-your-country). The cost of the design, from the keys article: everything that matters is in the key, which is why key management is where the effort goes now.

sources.where: From the data to the keys
In short; Where everything lives

idea:a-password-manager-and-a-registry.title: Where the keys live: a password manager for the keys a person holds, a registry vault for the keys agents make
idea:a-password-manager-and-a-registry.statement: Once agents create vaults several times a day, keeping the keys by hand stops working. The keys a person holds go in a password manager, which is and will stay the preferred home; everything the agents create goes to a registry, a private vault run by its own isolated Claude session with no other access, the vault of vaults, so a key is never lost and never has to live in a browser tab or a chat. Remembering keys under aliases on one machine is a convenience, not a management system. The weakest step is giving a key to another agent, because the agent platforms have no secrets per session.
idea:a-password-manager-and-a-registry.notes: State at sgit-ai v0.20.0, 10 October 2026. The gap, quoted from the platform's docs: on Claude Code on the web an environment variable is one 'any command Claude runs can read' and 'Anyone who uses the environment can read the values'; a network secret keeps the key outside the VM but is per environment and cannot help with a vault key, because decryption happens inside the session; Codex removes its secrets before the agent phase starts. So a key for another agent travels in the prompt (a transcript), in an environment variable (every session reads it), or not at all, with the agent making its own vault and sending the key back on a lane, the pattern used most. The four tracks next: password manager integrations (an open call published, not followed up yet), secrets.sgit.ai (a keyring unlocked by a passkey's PRF output, a 128-bit recovery code shown once, at v0.1.13 the design and a lab shipped and the app proposed), PKI (RFC 0001), and decryption out of band (an idea, not a design).

sources.where: Where the vault keys are kept today; The weakest step: giving a key to an agent; What comes next

idea:small-vaults-for-small-jobs.title: A vault per conversation and per job: a leaked key exposes one small thing, not an inbox
idea:small-vaults-for-small-jobs.statement: Working this way you start making very small vaults for very specific things: a communication vault for the two or three agents on a job, in which they talk and work through versioned, encrypted files. What an agent needs to join one is small: the vault key, sgit and network access to one host, or a server inside its own network. This is the right shape for security: a leaked key exposes one small vault and one conversation, not an inbox, a drive or an account, and every word is on the record for the person who holds the keys. It is also why the number of keys grew faster than one person could manage by hand.
idea:small-vaults-for-small-jobs.notes: Pairs with an-agent-is-a-session-with-a-focus (one session per topic) and with the main workflow the article describes: give Claude no permissions and no access to anything, only the vault it uses to communicate, or a vault it creates and the person then captures. Inside the vaults the agents use EmailFS and IssuesFS, file-based protocols for mail and issues.

sources.where: Small vaults for small jobs

idea:write-only-lanes.title: Append lanes: one POST from anywhere, readable only by the vault's owner
idea:write-only-lanes.statement: A lane is a write-only channel attached to a vault. A sender holds a token for one lane and the owner's public key, seals its message to that key and sends it with a single POST; the owner decrypts with a private key that never leaves them, and the server keeps only hashes and ciphertext, so compromising it yields hashes and ciphertext. One lane per sender, so one can be revoked without touching the others. It is used for key handover, for logs and observations from sessions that hold no vault key, for what a reader fills in on a web page, and for messages between agents on different platforms with different owners. A little like email, and the token is still a secret: it cannot read, but with the vault id it authorises writes.
idea:write-only-lanes.notes: This is the piece that lets a site with no server take input: the newsroom's newsletter sign-ups and shared reading go through the same encrypted, write-only inbox (no-server-by-design), and the agent desktop design sends outputs and the footprint to a vault the desktop can append to and cannot rewrite. The no-server article notes it is the one part of the vault server that needs a small piece of server logic.

sources.where: Append lanes, the transport behind most of this

idea:nobody-buys-it-for-the-encryption.title: Nobody buys it for the encryption: the features came from the constraint
idea:nobody-buys-it-for-the-encryption.statement: Encryption is an important property, not a reason to choose a tool, and leading with it was a mistake Dinis made himself: if sgit succeeds it will be because it has better features and better workflows. Many of those came from the encryption as a constraint, because innovation needs constraints and the loop of trying, failing and shipping; the research is more careful than the slogan, an inverted U-shaped effect, some constraint helps and too much hurts. The same applies to design: take things away until it hurts, and stop there; the best product is not the one you use because you have to but the one that hurts when you stop.
idea:nobody-buys-it-for-the-encryption.notes: The research named is Acar, Tarakci and van Knippenberg, Creativity and innovation under constraints, Journal of Management, 2019, quoted: 'an inverted U-shaped effect of constraints on creativity and innovation'. Dinis declares a stake: sgit is his, and the article says the market will decide. A line for the cutter too: 'take things away until it hurts, and stop there, because past that point it gets worse.' Tension to watch with ship-now-ship-serverless, which presents SG/Send and sgit by their privacy property: the book should sell them by the workflow and name the privacy as the property.

sources.where: The mistake I made first; Open source, as a constraint

idea:encryption-does-not-remove-gdpr.title: Client-side encryption reduces the exposure under GDPR; it does not take you out of it
idea:encryption-does-not-remove-gdpr.statement: Dinis's memo said that with the data encrypted you do not have to worry about GDPR, and the article corrects it: for whoever holds the keys, encrypted personal data is still personal data, storing it is still processing, and the controller's duties stay (the UK regulator says not to think encrypted data is outside the UK GDPR). What encryption does is reduce the exposure, and the law recognises it: Article 32 lists encryption as a security measure, and under Article 34(3)(a) a breach need not be communicated to the people affected if the data was made unintelligible to anyone not authorised, provided the key was not lost with it. The Court of Justice held in September 2025 that pseudonymised data is not personal data in all cases and for every person, which may help a store that never has the keys. Much less to worry about, not nothing.
idea:encryption-does-not-remove-gdpr.notes: An instance of asked-to-be-corrected: the memo's claim stands corrected in the article, and the book must not repeat the memo. Sources named in the article: GDPR Articles 32 and 34; ICO encryption guidance; Court of Justice case C-413/23 P, press release of 4 September 2025. Not legal advice. Answers the 2018 outline GDPR, which the map says no article covered for developers.

sources.where: What it does not do: GDPR

idea:open-source-all-of-it-or-it-is-an-e.title: Open source as a constraint: all of it, or it is an evaluation version with a better name
idea:open-source-all-of-it-or-it-is-an-e.statement: The constraint is that there is no private code. It makes the code easy to deploy, run and change, including by the customer, which solves many sovereignty problems on its own, and it removes two temptations: to lock the customer in, and the curse of most startups, building every feature and integration one customer wants until the roadmap belongs to everyone but the startup. With open source the answer is: here is the code, integrate it yourself or pay us to do that specific thing. That is why you cannot open source half of it: a community edition that turns proprietary when you use it for real is an evaluation version, and Elastic, HashiCorp and Redis each moved to a non-open licence and each produced a well-funded fork (OpenSearch, OpenTofu, Valkey). The business model that follows is selling customisation and keeping it working.
idea:open-source-all-of-it-or-it-is-an-e.notes: Distinct from the-fork-next-door (the fork as protection) and open-source-removes-the-moat-excuse (why it is easy to throw your own technology away): this is the founder's business reason for all of it. Elastic (29 August 2024) and Redis (1 May 2025) have since added an open licence back; the Open Source Initiative said the SSPL is not an open source licence (19 January 2021). The article's own limit: that small teams win this way is Dinis's view from what he sees, not a study. The constraints remove bad business decisions and leave the good one: if the code is open and the server holds nothing, you cannot sell access to the code or rent the data back.

sources.where: Open source, as a constraint; All of it, or it is an evaluation version; The business model that follows

idea:what-serverless-costs-when-idle.title: What serverless costs when nobody is using it, product by product, 18 October 2026
idea:what-serverless-costs-when-idle.statement: From the products' own pricing pages on 18 October 2026, excluding storage, at 730 hours and US East rates: Lambda event functions, Cloud Run, Cosmos DB serverless, Neon and Redshift Serverless cost zero idle; Aurora Serverless v2 zero since November 2024 and OpenSearch's next-generation collections zero since May 2026. MSK Serverless bills $0.75 per cluster-hour, about $550 a month idle; OpenSearch classic collections have a floor of two capacity units, about $350 a month; Neptune Serverless a floor of one capacity unit, about $80 a month; ElastiCache Serverless a minimum of storage metered hourly, from $6 a month. The definitions were clear: the CNCF's whitepaper says 'there is no charge when code is not running', and the Berkeley paper warned in 2019 that few so-called elastic services could scale to zero.
idea:what-serverless-costs-when-idle.notes: The monthly figures are Dinis's arithmetic and move with region and configuration; the article says so. Some floors have fallen over time: Aurora Serverless v2 had a floor of half a capacity unit, priced in 2022 at 'just shy of $45' a month, until scale to zero arrived in November 2024; OpenSearch Serverless started at four units, halved in June 2024, reached zero in May 2026. For the hands-on chapter the table is a dated figure to renew each year; the test it supports (ship-now-ship-serverless) does not date.

sources.where: What it means now (the table); What serverless meant

idea:the-glue-behind-the-commodity.title: The name shows the glue: a first version is often a villager's work dressed as a town planner's
idea:the-glue-behind-the-commodity.statement: Naming a service as ephemeral, town planner and a service makes you ask whether it is really a commodity or only looks like one, and plenty of things sold as commodities are a large amount of custom technology glued together behind the scenes. Lambda, the definition of serverless for most people, ran on Linux containers inside EC2 instances for its first four years, until Firecracker replaced them from 2018, in its builders' own words. A per-hour bill for a 'serverless' product usually means the provider cannot yet spin the thing up and down fast and safely enough to bill by use: an engineering gap on their side, passed to you as a cost. Not a criticism, that is how services become commodities, and the floors that halve and the scale-to-zero that arrives are the record of it maturing in public.
idea:the-glue-behind-the-commodity.notes: Could also serve where-do-you-land as a worked example of a Wardley map showing what sits behind a commodity. Werner Vogels is quoted: AWS delivers 'new services often with a minimal feature set' and lets customers 'help drive the roadmap'. The Firecracker account is AWS's own (NSDI 2020). Wardley in 2016: 'It's not really serverless but more I don't care what a server is.'

sources.where: The test; The glue behind the commodity

idea:the-code-must-not-know-it-moved.title: Move the cloud, not the code: a twin the application cannot tell from the real service
idea:the-code-must-not-know-it-moved.statement: Workloads stay on hyperscalers because moving means changing code: every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is written into applications that work today and nobody wants to touch. So the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved. The same calls land on a twin, an open source interface to a real system valued for one thing, that the client cannot tell the difference, and the twin decides where the bytes go: real S3, an sgit vault, a European operator's data centre, a laptop. Switching a mock costs a code path; switching a twin costs an endpoint, so migration becomes a configuration decision rather than a project, and projects get cancelled. The S3 twin exists as open source; EC2 and IAM do not yet.
idea:the-code-must-not-know-it-moved.notes: Dated 12 October 2026, from a digital sovereignty event; the chief executive is not named and did not review it. AWS's European Sovereign Cloud went live on 15 January 2026, a separate cloud with its first region in Brandenburg, operated by EU residents; the article's reading: 'Sovereignty that depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission.' None of it works if the twin layer is closed: swap one vendor's API for another vendor's proprietary wrapper and the lock-in has moved, not gone.

sources.where: Why workloads do not move; The criterion: the code must not know; This is not theoretical: the S3 twin

idea:sovereignty-never-signs-a-migration.title: The reason to move is never sovereignty or cost: sell value that lands the day they switch
idea:sovereignty-never-signs-a-migration.statement: Sovereignty and cost reduction are important and never urgent; they sit on the risk register under important, not urgent, and nobody signs the risk of a migration for a principle or for a return that depends on a future event. The person signing needs value that lands the day they switch and gives them cover if it goes wrong: backups that exist, every object version controlled, encryption the operator cannot read with the key held by the customer, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip, cost per workload visible before the invoice, and an item taken off the top of the register. 'It is in Europe now' is not a decision somebody can defend. For an operator in Romania, Portugal or the UK, 'move to us' sells risk; 'keep your code, point it at us, and come out with versions, encryption, a journal and policies' sells value with the risk removed.
idea:sovereignty-never-signs-a-migration.notes: A selling lesson in general form: find the return that closes before the risk does, and the buyer who owns that register line rather than the cloud bill. The article says its value list is 'still a little invisible to a signer' and needs sharpening; the business model's numbers are labelled assumptions, shapes not quotes, for somebody else to run. The margin is in the twin layer (journal, policy enforcement, reports a regulator or insurer accepts), not in storage and compute, which are commodities: the same reading as why-i-love-wardley-maps.

sources.where: The reason to move is never sovereignty; The business model

idea:no-new-features-during-the-move.title: A villager move: no new features while you move, or nobody can tell which change broke what
idea:no-new-features-during-the-move.statement: A migration is a pure villager move, from explorer to town planner: take something that works and make it boring, reliable and cheap, without changing what it does. The temptation to add features during it is the moment everything derails, because the migration is now also a product change and nobody can tell which of the two broke what. The argument that the move is what allows the features is right, and it is exactly why the two must not be mixed: move first, with the code unmodified and the twin adding its value underneath, then add the features the move made possible.
idea:no-new-features-during-the-move.notes: The same rule the newsroom used for its own explorer-to-villager move (green-does-not-mean-live cites it): same bytes and same bugs first, features after. Could sit in shipped-means-the-user-has-it instead.

idea:run-unmodified-against-a-twin.title: Every piece of software should run, unmodified, against a twin of every service it depends on
idea:run-unmodified-against-a-twin.statement: If the application cannot tell a twin from the real service, the same unmodified code can run against an in-memory twin in milliseconds on a laptop, against a twin replaying last week's production journal, against a twin injecting the failures staging never shows (a timeout, a throttle, a permission that disappears halfway through a job), and against the real service for the final check. Most teams test against mocks they wrote themselves and hope production behaves the same; with twins the environment becomes a setting rather than a guess. Software that can only run against one provider's live API is software you cannot test properly, cannot move, and cannot put a policy in front of.
idea:run-unmodified-against-a-twin.notes: A side effect the article says 'may end up mattering more than sovereignty'. The twin is also where the journal and the behaviour policy live, because every call passes through it (mandate-reach-gap, one-way-two-way-doors). The 2018 Chaos Engineering outline is the failure-injection half of this.

idea:startup-credits-october-2026.title: The startup credit programmes, as their pages read on 7 October 2026
idea:startup-credits-october-2026.statement: All amounts and criteria read from each programme's own page on 7 October 2026. AWS Activate Founders: $1,000, up to $5,000, for self-funded, pre-Series B companies founded in the last 10 years on the Paid Tier plan; AWS Activate Portfolio: up to $200,000, through an Activate Provider (an investor or accelerator), pre-Series B. Microsoft for Startups: up to $150K over time, for a for-profit software company before Series C with under $350K lifetime Azure credits. Google for Startups Cloud: $2,000 pre-funding, up to $350,000 for AI startups, seed to Series A, founded in the last 5 years, under $5K prior credits. Anthropic's startup programme: $1,000 API credits, a year of Claude Team and up to $45K in partner offers, for companies founded in the last 5 years or funded in the last 2. Also: E2B $20,000 one-time plus the Pro tier; Daytona $10K immediately, up to $100K; Scaleway Founders up to 1,000 euros over 12 months and Early Stage 9,000 euros (1,500 a month for 6 months); Cloudflare for Startups $10K, $100K or $350K by tier; Modal unspecified thousands. Programmes change; check before applying.
idea:startup-credits-october-2026.notes: The full table, as the article prints it. E2B, E2B for Startups: $20,000 one-time, plus the Pro tier; under 3 years old, raised under $5M, first-time E2B user, building AI agents; e2b.dev/startups/apply. Daytona, Startup Grid: $10K immediately, up to $100K; eligibility not published, the form asks for funding stage and VC partner; daytona.io/startups. Scaleway, Founders: up to 1,000 euros over 12 months; under 5 years old, under 50 staff, not yet a Scaleway customer; form on the Founders page, startup-program@scaleway.com. Scaleway, Early Stage: 9,000 euros (1,500 euros a month for 6 months); as Founders, with at least 500 euros a month of consumption; form on the Early Stage page. AWS, Activate Founders: $1,000, up to $5,000; self-funded, pre-Series B, founded in the last 10 years, account on the Paid Tier plan; aws.amazon.com/startups. AWS, Activate Portfolio: up to $200,000; through an Activate Provider (an investor or accelerator), pre-Series B; same link, with the provider's Org ID. Microsoft, Microsoft for Startups: up to $150K over time; for-profit software company, before Series C, under $350K lifetime Azure credits; startups.microsoft.com. Google Cloud, Google for Startups Cloud: $2,000 pre-funding; up to $350,000 for AI startups; seed to Series A, founded in the last 5 years, under $5K prior credits; cloud.google.com/startup/apply. Cloudflare, Cloudflare for Startups: $10K, $100K or $350K by tier; by funding tier, first-time applicants, business email; cloudflare.com/lp/startups. Modal, Modal for Startups: unspecified 'thousands' in credits; new to Modal, VC-funded through a partner or over $1M raised; modal.com/startups. Anthropic, Startup programme: $1,000 API credits, a year of Claude Team, up to $45K in partner offers; founded in the last 5 years or funded in the last 2; platform.claude.com/offers/startups-application. Two that look like startup programmes are not, for this purpose: MacStadium's open-source programme (a free Mac mini for unpaid maintainers; a commercial product does not qualify and should not be dressed up as one) and Hetzner's referral credit, which could not be confirmed from an official page on the day. Dinis's gen-zx article calls this 'the only table of startup cloud credits (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Anthropic)'; the table also carries E2B, Daytona, Scaleway, Cloudflare and Modal. The ElevenLabs grants programme (twelve months, 33 million characters, companies under 25 people with a monetised use; characters cannot be exchanged or resold) and AssemblyAI's twelve months of recurring credits are in the-key-is-the-billing-system, read on 12 October 2026, and belong in the same chapter.

idea:apply-with-the-work-as-the-applicat.title: Apply only where you meet the criteria, with the page that says what you would do, and publish the results
idea:apply-with-the-work-as-the-applicat.statement: Before applying to a credit programme, check each criterion against your own age, funding and customer status, and apply only where they are met; do not dress a commercial product up as an open-source project to fit a programme that is not for it. Apply with the published page that describes what you would do with the credits, and offer the provider the result: the same tasks run on their product next to the others, measured rather than read, published with the gaps. Ask the questions the programme pages do not answer before relying on them (what the credits cover, when they expire, whether a monthly fee is paid from them).
idea:apply-with-the-work-as-the-applicat.notes: The billing article adds the method for writing to providers: principles first, one sentence as the ask, send the research already done ('a provider that can see the research already done tends to answer the question that was actually asked'), agents draft and the founder sends, and every answer recorded as an issue with its date.

idea:the-model-cannot-be-the-barrier.title: The desktop is the barrier, not the model: prompt injection is not solved, so the box has to hold
idea:the-model-cannot-be-the-barrier.statement: Anthropic's own measurements of prompt injection in browser use went from a 23.6% attack success rate without mitigations to 11.2% in August 2025 and to about 1% in November 2025, a rate that in their words 'still represents meaningful risk'; Brave showed in October 2025 that nearly invisible text in screenshots could hijack agentic browsers; OpenAI wrote that it is unlikely ever to be fully solved. A desktop shows an agent pages, documents and emails written by other people, so over a working month the question is not whether a page will try but what the agent can do when one succeeds. An egress allowlist limits where it can send, a box without secrets limits what it can send, a revocable identity limits for how long, a recording says what happened; the model's defences reduce how often that matters and do not replace it. One mandate per task, written before the desktop exists, and the desktop configured from it.
idea:the-model-cannot-be-the-barrier.notes: The nine properties of a locked-down agent desktop: isolation, an egress allowlist, secrets kept outside, an identity of its own, a live view and takeover, a record, a clean reset, billing that follows the work, the right desktop. On 7 October 2026 every one could be bought somewhere and no single product had all nine; the three that stop a hijacked agent doing damage (allowlist, secrets outside, own identity) were documented on one product, with two of them in private beta there. The OpenAI quote is from news coverage. Extends mandate-reach-gap and not-on-your-laptop with the desktop case.

sources.where: The model cannot be the barrier; What locked down means; What we would build from what exists

idea:a-vault-server-in-83-lines.title: A read-only vault needs no code; a read-write vault server is 83 lines on a free plan
idea:a-vault-server-in-83-lines.statement: Because the sgit server never sees a key or a plaintext byte, it has almost nothing to do, and that is what the test showed on 18 October 2026. Read-only: no code at all; sgit publish writes a folder any static host can serve, and the real client cloned it back identically. Read-write: one Worker of 83 lines, one R2 bucket and one Durable Object per vault, all on Cloudflare's free plan, run in Cloudflare's own runtime locally with the real client: create, push, clone; a stale push that merged; two pushes at once where one was told nothing was overwritten; a read-only clone that refused to write; a wrong write key answered 403; and no plaintext anywhere in what the server stored. It has not yet run on a real account, does not do files over 4 MB, and has one shared access token.
idea:a-vault-server-in-83-lines.notes: The value of constraints in practice, in the article's own words: 'because the server can read nothing, it has almost nothing to do.' A nuance for the book's 'no servers of mine with logic in them': the 83 lines are logic of yours, the small commodity function the no-server article allows for the one real limit (writes that must be checked). The Worker and its wrangler configuration are printed in full in the article, so the weekend chapter can point at them rather than reprint them.

sources.where: An sgit vault on Cloudflare

idea:reach-is-a-computed-value.title: Reach is a computed value, and new capability lands as excess, never as new authority
idea:reach-is-a-computed-value.statement: What an agent can reach is not a document but the output of a calculation, so the question to answer is what calculates it and whether that is a one-time snapshot or wired to the pipeline. When a connector or integration is added the reach grows, the gap recomputes and a re-review follows; the mandate is locked business logic that changes only through change control, so a new capability can only land in the gap as excess, never as new authority. Unbounded includes volume: an agent permitted £10k per action that can perform a thousand actions carries a £10m exposure.
idea:reach-is-a-computed-value.notes: Status in the article: MVPs and proofs of concept, complete for simple single-agent deployments. The question's example is in dollars ($25k cap, $75k order) and the answer's in pounds (£10k mandate, £100k reach); the book should pick one currency.

sources.where: 2. How do we keep behaviour policies current as agents gain new powers?; 1. What happens when an agent bypasses its behaviour policy?

idea:who-can-pull-the-plug.title: Who can pull the plug: an agent that cannot be stopped is riskier than one that can
idea:who-can-pull-the-plug.statement: Most AI projects do not fail technically; they stall when the business finally asks the good questions: can you stop it, what if it issues ten thousand of something, who is liable. Every board asks the same question about an agent in one sentence, who can pull the plug, how fast, what breaks and what cannot be undone, and a deployed agent's risk cannot be denied, only accepted by a named owner for an interval with an expiry. An agent that cannot be stopped is far riskier than one that can; containment (terminate, revoke, block, quarantine, ticket) is designed in advance and executed by the company's own stack.
idea:who-can-pull-the-plug.notes: RiskMandate's position as the article states it: not inline, not an insurer, not a one-button solution; it 'makes agents insurable' and does not insure them; no risk transfer exists today.

sources.where: 4. How are we insuring or assuring agent behaviour?, 'An audit trail is not a guarantee'; 8. Remediation when a policy is bypassed; 10. Measurable business and technical outcomes, Getting to production
How does it get into the room?, the board's risk appetite

idea:sell-the-build-not-the-code.title: Open source everything, and sell the customised, tested, maintained build
idea:sell-the-build-not-the-code.statement: Everything the company builds is open source, with no proprietary layer; what the customer buys is a build for them, sometimes with fewer features and so less attack surface, tested on their target, maintained as models, connectors and threats change, with someone accountable for it, and cheaper through you than doing it themselves. Not a donation, and not a licence that gives you a reason to make the free version worse. In the article's simulation, customised builds for companies cover one project's long-tail cost in 94% of draws, donations in 24%, and about £1.80 a machine a year from individuals covers it in half the draws with typical conversion; no price reaches nine in ten.
idea:sell-the-build-not-the-code.notes: The article says the model is a model, not a forecast, and that the three assumptions that move it most (how many machines are out there, willingness to pay, the share on the long tail) are not well measured in public data. Quote worth keeping: 'The value is the support, not the code, so the code can stay open.' The ten-questions article calls the moat 'delivery, maintenance and trust', not lock-in.

sources.where: What this says; Five ways to pay for the long tail, simulated; What price pays for the long tail?

idea:answer-the-hard-questions-and-check.title: Answer the hard questions in full, publish what is live and what is design, and check your own site against the answers
idea:answer-the-hard-questions-and-check.statement: When a buyer's, investor's or competitor's hard questions come back from a conference, answer them in one structured interview with an agent acting as a journalist that challenges every answer until the set holds together; publish an honest maturity table of what is live and what is design; and check the answers against what the company has already published. The exercise found three contradictions on RiskMandate's own site: a homepage saying 'enforced in real time', an insurance page in the present tense for things that were design, and a Level 1 price of £10 on two pages and £5 on a third.
idea:answer-the-hard-questions-and-check.notes: Could also sit in facts-and-the-record; placed in sell because the questions are a buyer's. The line that closes the set: 'Where we are early, we say so.'

sources.where: Where this comes from; Honest maturity, across all ten; Three things this exercise showed we must fix on our own site

idea:a-policy-beside-the-prompt.title: A third input: a behaviour policy beside the system prompt and the prompt, which the vendor acknowledges, enforces where it can and answers for
idea:a-policy-beside-the-prompt.statement: An agent today gets a system prompt from its vendor and a prompt from us; it should also take an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor accepts as part of the deployment, enforces as far as the platform can see, reports every breach against the same day and, eventually, carries liability for the rows it accepted. The user answers for what is outside the policy and the vendor for what is inside it, which is a better model than the user being liable for everything because they clicked allow. Most agents already run a hidden policy of their own (Claude in Chrome will not type a password), and a system prompt is a light behaviour policy not written as one; the layering is the vendor's published policy, then the deployer's, with the business logic only the deployer can write.
idea:a-policy-beside-the-prompt.notes: A proposal: the article says no vendor accepts a behaviour policy as an input today in this sense; Claude Code's permission rules and managed settings are the nearest thing and cover settings, not business rules. Liability per row is the end state, not the start; acknowledgement and breach reporting can come first.

sources.where: The idea: a policy beside the prompt; The user answers outside the policy, the vendor inside it; A system prompt is a light behaviour policy; Most agents already run a policy

idea:code-and-data-in-one-channel.title: Models do not separate code from data, so a rule in the prompt can be argued with by an email
idea:code-and-data-in-one-channel.statement: In a computer the instructions and the data they operate on are kept apart, and most of the worst security bugs in history, from buffer overflows to SQL injection, are what happens when that separation breaks; in a language model there is no separation to break, every instruction and every piece of content arrives in the same channel, and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre said in December 2025 that prompt injection may never be mitigated the way SQL injection was. A behaviour policy does not fix this; it moves the most important instructions, what the agent may do, into a channel the content cannot reach, loaded by the platform, versioned, signed and checked outside the model where it can be.
idea:code-and-data-in-one-channel.notes: Sits beside secrets-never-in-the-chat (the lethal trifecta) and is the reason mandate-reach-gap calls a rule in a prompt hope. Quote worth keeping, Simon Willison's: 'LLMs follow instructions in content'.

sources.where: The old problem: code and data in one channel; What this does not claim

idea:aviation-and-payments-got-safe-when.title: Aviation and payments got safe when the rule, the liability and the business model pointed the same way
idea:aviation-and-payments-got-safe-when.statement: Aviation did not get safe out of altruism but because every crash became news: at 1995's rate of 2.72 fatal airliner accidents per million flights, 2025's 38.7 million flights would have meant about 105 fatal accidents; there were 12. Payments got some of the best security teams anywhere because the liability was moved onto the companies: a US cardholder liable for at most $50 since 1970, £35 in the UK, the 2015 liability shift onto whoever had not adopted chip cards, the PCI council founded by the card brands in 2006, and UK banks reimbursing scam victims up to £85,000 since October 2024, after which losses fell by around 21%. Regulation alone does not do it (Meta's €1.2 billion GDPR fine in 2023, €200 million in 2025); the improvement comes where a rule, a liability that lands on the company and a systemic risk to the business model line up, and agents can be that case.
idea:aviation-and-payments-got-safe-when.notes: The article's own caveats: the aviation numbers mix sources (Aviation Safety Network via Our World in Data, the Flight Safety Foundation, IATA); the 21% fall is one evaluation's estimate; 'it does not take many users' to lose trust in agents is Dinis's judgement with no number behind it.

sources.where: Aviation did not get safe out of altruism; Payments got safe because liability moved; Regulation alone does not do it

idea:the-policy-is-the-business-logic.title: Zoom into an agent's behaviour policy and you find the business logic, which only the business can write
idea:the-policy-is-the-business-logic.statement: The first rules anybody writes for an agent are mechanical and the same in every company: do not send, only draft; do not delete; use your own account. A few questions in (which drafts may it send, can it mention a price, can it chase an invoice finance has not approved, can it write to a client in dispute) you are describing the business, in layers with different owners: the function, the process, the relationship, and what the company is for. Vendors stop at the mechanics by the shape of the problem, since a vendor that models each customer's business becomes a consultancy; the business layers are the customer's to write, and written together with skills (a skill says how, a policy layer says what is allowed, who owns the rule and what stands in the way) they are the business codified for an agent, which is what lets a company hand it real work and scale.
idea:the-policy-is-the-business-logic.notes: The article's own five readers flag that its front matter overstates the body: 'the only way to describe agent behaviour at the granularity a business actually runs at' is unsupported; the body says only that a fractal structure is the one Dinis found that can hold it. The register should not say 'only way'. The firm, its rules and its counts are fictional on purpose.

sources.where: Above the mechanics is the business; Why the vendors stop at the mechanics; It looks a lot like a skill

idea:software-was-the-law.title: Software was the law: the rule the screen enforced by omission is no longer enforced once an agent calls the API
idea:software-was-the-law.statement: Companies never wrote their business logic down because they did not need to: a clerk could not send an unapproved invoice because the finance system had no button for it until the approval was recorded, and a support agent could not see payment details because their role did not include the screen. An agent works through APIs, not screens, and can call the endpoint the button would have called, so the rule the user interface enforced by omission is no longer enforced unless somebody writes it down and something enforces it; the behaviour policy is where it gets written down.
idea:software-was-the-law.notes: The Historian's reading of the article calls this its nugget: 'every later article is about the "something enforces it" half.' Approval chains, RBAC, field-level permissions and workflow engines are where privacy decisions and much of practical governance live.

sources.where: Software was the law

idea:control-accepted-risk-or-hope.title: Every rule lands in one of three states: backed by a control, governed by an accepted risk, or resting on hope
idea:control-accepted-risk-or-hope.statement: For each rule the policy records what stands in the way: nothing, an expectation (a rule in prose, enforced by nobody), a setting the agent's own account can flip, or a boundary enforced above it, and only the boundary is a control. Add one more fact, whether a named person has accepted the risk of the rule not being enforced, with an expiry, and every rule is a control, an accepted risk or hope, which can be counted. In the article's fictional firm 5 of 17 rules are backed by a control, 6 by an accepted risk and 6 by hope; the platform layer is all control, the organisation layer all hope, and each existing product (a send gateway, an outbound content check, a blocked-recipients list) moves one row.
idea:control-accepted-risk-or-hope.notes: Adds the third state, accepted risk, to mandate-reach-gap's hope versus enforcement. The proportions are illustrative; the article says the shape is the point. Resting on hope is not a failure, most of a business has always run on people behaving as asked, but with an agent it can be counted.

sources.where: How much of it is hope?; Where the vendors plug in

idea:open-source-is-not-free.title: Open source is not free: somebody pays, and the people who get the value have no easy way to
idea:open-source-is-not-free.statement: Somebody is paying for open source, even if only with their time. The long tail is measurable and not small: 6.99% of Homebrew's macOS install events in the last 30 days, and 16.66% over a year, came from versions older than the newest three, and 18.55% of pip downloads run on end-of-life Python. Money flows to old versions when a vendor owns them (Oracle earned $19.8 billion from support last year; Red Hat's subscriptions ran at about 93% gross margin) and not when a community does: open source receives about 0.09% of its estimated value in investment, and 60% of maintainers describe themselves as unpaid hobbyists. The question was never whether somebody pays; it is whether the people who get the value have an easy way to pay for it.
idea:open-source-is-not-free.notes: The case that started it: an Intel iMac clean-installed with macOS 13 for Dinis's agents could not run Homebrew or Docker Desktop and needed Python by hand; the research corrected the story (only the 2017 iMacs stop at Ventura; Homebrew now refuses the CPU, not just the OS). The xz maintainer wrote 'this is an unpaid hobby project' two years before the backdoor.

sources.where: In short; The long tail, measured; Where the money flows

idea:pence-only-work-aggregated.title: Below about five pounds the card fee is the price, so pence payments only work aggregated
idea:pence-only-work-aggregated.statement: Stripe's standard UK rate is 1.5% plus 20p: on a £20 payment that is 2.5%, on £5 it is 5.5%, on 50p it is 41.5%, and on 10p it is more than the payment. So payments of pence only work aggregated: one charge a year that covers many projects, or a platform that already holds a balance and settles in bulk, which is how the newsroom's reading meter prices a page at a few pence against £5 of credit settled as one balance. Payment also has to be tied to a verified user who receives something, not to a count: when tea.xyz rewarded package popularity with tokens, one developer published nearly 14,000 packages.
idea:pence-only-work-aggregated.notes: The article finds the card-versus-platform difference smaller than expected at £2 to £3, where the 20p fee is under 10%; aggregation matters below about £1.

sources.where: The pence problem; Why not just charge?, Per-install rewards get gamed

idea:the-agents-leave-a-record.title: 'Nobody knows how it is built' is fixable: make the agents leave a record, a mandate, a memory and a graph
idea:the-agents-leave-a-record.statement: HBR's warning that the AI designs the architecture so nobody in-house knows how the tool is built is true of most agent-built software today and does not have to be. If the agents work under a written mandate, keep their memory in a versioned store the company owns, and describe what they built as a graph, the architecture is a record the next team can read, not a mystery. A prototype ready for the villagers looks like Mondweep Chakravorty's SGit and Ruflo run: versions pinned, sixteen tests, a folder of evidence, a written behaviour policy, and a README that says plainly what it does not do yet.
idea:the-agents-leave-a-record.notes: The article says the record is a proposal, not a standard: this site runs it; few organisations do yet. Dinis declares a stake: his companies sell open source and this kind of record.

sources.where: 'Nobody knows how it is built' can be fixed

idea:the-bonus-test-is-accountability.title: The bonus test: if nobody will put their name or their bonus on it in production, it is not ready to be in line
idea:the-bonus-test-is-accountability.statement: HBR's test for a chief executive, would your team accept a bonus tied to how this tool performs in production, is the town planner's accountability by another name: the moment someone takes the code and answers for it. The industry already says whoever ships code is responsible for it however it was written: the Linux kernel's rules say AI agents must not add Signed-off-by tags and only humans can certify the Developer Certificate of Origin, and Fedora's proposal says the contributor is always the author and fully accountable. An explorer cannot be made accountable for code they never read; the team the work is handed to can, and the town planners above all.

idea:lithuania-two-lines.title: What the newsroom says about Lithuania and the Portuguese company, as of 12 October 2026: two lines
idea:lithuania-two-lines.statement: The company Dinis created in Portugal for MyFeeds is being closed, because running a company with little revenue in Portugal is expensive in a way it is not in England; he is looking at Lithuania for the next one, for its digital advantages. The article's own limit: the company move is a consideration, not a decision; Lithuania is being looked at and nothing has been registered.
idea:lithuania-two-lines.notes: This is all the newsroom has on Lithuania and on the Portuguese company. It is the evidence behind the Lithuania and Portugal lines of the-company-itself-for-real until the journalist's gap articles arrive; the book should not say more than this from this source.

idea:the-thinking-is-never-wasted.title: The thinking is never wasted: pause in the open and pick up when the moment comes
idea:the-thinking-is-never-wasted.statement: The Cyber Boardroom, a GenAI platform for boards with an advisor called Athena, taught Dinis what personas and customised output are worth and paused because nobody wants confidential board material in an environment somebody else runs; what it needed is what he later built as sgit. MyFeeds built personalised feeds on semantic graphs, found the industry silent on graphs, micropayments and paying the people who write, and paused. The 2025 writing on monetising trust, fact provenance and micro and nano payments is what the newsroom now stands on, and he is going back to the publishers with an end-to-end example; if it does not land in 2026 he will try in 2027. Because it was open and written down, it was there when the moment came.
idea:the-thinking-is-never-wasted.notes: The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds are summarised from memory in the article, and the proofs of concept are not all published. For the founder it illustrates connect-the-dots-backwards: a pivot leaves assets when it is done in the open.

idea:your-newsroom-is-your-demo-and-your.title: Your own newsroom is the public example of your product, and underneath it a CRM and a publishing workflow
idea:your-newsroom-is-your-demo-and-your.statement: The hardest part of selling behaviour policies and licences to operate is showing them in action, because customer work cannot be shared; the ecosystem around the newsroom, its agents, their behaviour policy, the status report every few answers, the leak scan before every commit, the releases with their logs, is the best public example RiskMandate has of a policy under real load every day. And a very effective newsroom is, underneath, a very effective CRM and publishing workflow: agents that follow up people and threads, draft, publish and keep a record, matured by readers in a way the product's own volumes could not yet force. Follow the users and the feedback loops, even when the user is you.
idea:your-newsroom-is-your-demo-and-your.notes: RiskMandate's traction is described, not measured, in the article.

sources.where: The newsroom is RiskMandate's workflow, and its example; Why the newsroom could solve it and RiskMandate could not

idea:not-ready-to-be-in-line.title: An explorer-coded app is a brief, not a product: not ready to be in line, and the further towards commodity the fewer agents in line
idea:not-ready-to-be-in-line.statement: An explorer-coded app may look and feel like an application, but nobody has read the code or validated the architecture, so it is not ready to be in line, in the path of work other people depend on. Dependence comes quickly: once something is used it is mission critical, even for one person if it replaced how they work, and from then on new versions cannot break it. The direction is set by where the code sits on the map: the further towards commodity, the fewer agents in line and the more deterministic the code; a model has no place in line on a mission-critical path.

idea:an-explorer-version-of-every-produc.title: Every product needs an explorer version, with paid conversions to a villager product and a town planner one
idea:an-explorer-version-of-every-produc.statement: Products need an explorer version in which users talk to the product with a model, reshape it, move things around and keep their own version, the product treated as primitives. When a user has something they want to keep they submit it, which is the brief, and pay to convert it into a villager product maintained across releases and, if it matters enough, a town planner product built properly or kept as a maintained fork. Each step is a revenue stream and each submission tells the vendor exactly what its users want; the same path should exist inside companies, between a department and its engineers, and around open-source projects, between users and maintainers.
idea:an-explorer-version-of-every-produc.notes: A proposal: the article knows of no vendor selling it. Could also sit in price-it-then-give-it-away as a pricing model; placed in the handover chapter because it is the handover, sold.

idea:twenty-minutes-with-your-own-assist.title: Write down what your agent can reach in twenty minutes: list its tools, say what you wanted it for, write the gap
idea:twenty-minutes-with-your-own-assist.statement: Few people have seen the list for their own agents. Paste the thirteen prompts from RiskMandate's try-it page into the assistant you already have connected to your mail: the first asks it to list its own tools ('the list is longer than the tile that sold it'), the second asks it to draft what you actually wanted it for in three lists, wanted, refused, never mentioned ('the correction is almost always downward'), the third writes the gap down. About twenty minutes, and nothing is collected. It is a self-report, the cheapest evidence there is and the weakest; a measured policy marks each row as measured, documented or inferred.

idea:answer-the-question-already-in-the-.title: Do not sell the need; answer a question somebody already has to answer, with a deadline
idea:answer-the-question-already-in-the-.statement: There are two groups, the people who see how fast agents are moving and the much larger group who do not, and the second group will not ask for an agent risk tool because they do not see the risk. The way in is a question somebody already has, with a deadline, in the language of the room: a contract, where legal and procurement ask what a vendor's agent will do with the data; a security questionnaire, where a startup's first serious enterprise customer asks which agents touch their data and how they are bounded; an insurance renewal, where the question is whether AI is excluded from cover; the board's risk appetite; and twenty minutes with the assistant you already run. None of these asks anyone to understand agents first.
idea:answer-the-question-already-in-the-.notes: A founder is on both sides: as the seller, and as the startup that, in the article's words, will be diligenced on its agents before long. The insurance argument is RiskMandate's, summarised from its pages, not independently surveyed.

idea:the-plumbing-is-the-states-road.title: The opportunity for a small country is the plumbing, built once by the state like a road, not the race for GPUs
idea:the-plumbing-is-the-states-road.statement: Frontier models, GPUs and data centres sit at the commodity end of the map with a lead a small country cannot buy back, so it should not enter that race. What stops a talented person in Braga or Cluj selling a service to the world is not talent, energy or price but forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in another language, a contract, an invoice, a tax form, each custom built every time in most of Europe when it should be infrastructure the state built once, like the road the shop did not pay for. In 2021, 18.5% of EU enterprises sold online to customers in their own country, 8.1% to other EU countries and 4.6% to the rest of the world. Estonia built the road: more than 142,000 e-residents and more than 43,000 companies, over 4,200 of them founded in 2026 by mid-September, on X-Road, open source under the MIT licence and connecting around a thousand organisations.
idea:the-plumbing-is-the-states-road.notes: Sharpens hack-your-country's 'judo for small countries' into the claim itself. The article says it is not a national strategy, the Eurostat figure is for 2021, and Estonia is a case study, not a template. For the founder it is the other side of the-company-itself: the plumbing a founder in the EU still builds alone.
